explanation: Ind AS 38 Paragraph 20 states that the nature of intangible assets is such that in many cases there are no additions to such an asset or replacements of part of it. Most subsequent expenditures are likely to maintain the expected future economic benefits embodied in an existing intangible asset rather than meet the definition of an intangible asset and the recognition criteria. Legal defense costs maintain existing rights and are expensed.

subject: Financial Reporting
tag: [ICAI CA Final FR PYQ] Ind AS 16: Decommissioning Obligation Change in Estimates
question: Coastal Refineries Ltd. measures its oil refinery using the Cost Model under Ind AS 16. In year 5, due to advanced green technology, the estimated present value of the decommissioning liability decreases by ₹8 Crores. How is this ₹8 Crores decrease accounted for under Appendix A of Ind AS 16 (Ind AS equivalent of IFRIC 1)?
options: Recognized immediately as a gain in Profit or Loss.
Deducted from the cost of the refinery asset in the current period; if the decrease exceeds the carrying amount of the asset, the excess is recognized immediately in profit or loss.
Credited directly to General Reserve.
Ignored until the refinery is finally decommissioned.
ref: Ind AS 16 - Appendix A (Changes in Existing Decommissioning, Restoration and Similar Liabilities)
explanation: Under Appendix A Paragraph 4, changes in the measurement of an existing decommissioning, restoration and similar liability that result from changes in the estimated timing or amount of the outflow of resources are added to, or deducted from, the cost of the related asset under the cost model. However, the amount deducted from the cost of the asset shall not exceed its carrying amount.

subject: Financial Reporting
tag: [ICAI CA Final FR PYQ] Ind AS 36: Indicators of Impairment
question: Which of the following is considered an external source of information indicating that an asset may be impaired under Ind AS 36?
options: Evidence is available of obsolescence or physical damage of an asset.

Significant changes with an adverse effect on the entity have taken place during the period, or are expected to take place in the near future, in the technological, market, economic, or legal environment in which the entity operates.
Internal reporting indicates that the economic performance of an asset is, or will be, worse than expected.
Significant restructuring plans for the division using the asset have been approved by management.
ref: Ind AS 36 - Paragraph 12(b): External Sources of Information for Impairment
explanation: Ind AS 36 Paragraph 12 divides indicators into external and internal sources. External sources include: significant unexpected declines in market value; significant adverse changes in technological, market, economic or legal environment; increases in market interest rates; and carrying amount of net assets exceeding market capitalization. Physical damage and internal reporting of poor performance are internal sources.

subject: Financial Reporting
tag: [ICAI CA Final FR PYQ] Ind AS 16: Cessation of Capitalisation of Borrowing Costs and Overheads
question: A commercial hotel building is structurally complete, fully furnished, licensed, and ready for occupancy on 30th November 2023. However, due to the upcoming tourist season in March 2024, management delays the grand opening until 1st March 2024. During this 3-month idle interval, management incurred security, staff training, and promotional expenses of ₹50 Lakhs. Can these costs be capitalized into the hotel PPE under Ind AS 16?
options: Yes, capitalization continues until the asset starts generating operating revenue from customers.

No, recognition of costs in the carrying amount of an item of PPE ceases when the item is in the location and condition necessary for it to be capable of operating in the manner intended by management; costs incurred while using or redeploying an item, initial operating losses, and promotional costs are expensed.
Yes, promotional expenses are mandatory components of initial cost.
Only the security costs can be capitalized.
ref: Ind AS 16 - Paragraph 20: Cessation of Capitalisation
explanation: Ind AS 16 Paragraph 20 states explicitly: 'Recognition of costs in the carrying amount of an item of property, plant and equipment ceases when the item is in the location and condition necessary for it to be capable of operating in the manner intended by management.' Costs incurred while an item capable of operating in the manner intended by management has yet to be brought into use, initial operating losses, and costs of introducing a new service are recognized in profit or loss.

subject: Financial Reporting
tag: [ICAI CA Final FR PYQ] Ind AS 115: 5-Step Model - Step 2 Distinct Performance Obligations
question: CloudTech Solutions Ltd. signs a single contract with a bank to: (i) grant a perpetual software license for core banking software; (ii) provide extensive custom code modifications so the software integrates with legacy payment switches; and (iii) provide 3 years of routine technical support. The custom modification significantly modifies the software code, and the software cannot function without this bespoke integration. How many performance obligations exist under Ind AS 115?
options: Three separate performance obligations: the software license, the custom modification service, and the technical support.

Two performance obligations: a combined performance obligation comprising the software license and custom modification service (because the software and customization are highly interrelated and represent a combined output), and a separate performance obligation for the 3-year technical support.
One single performance obligation comprising all three deliverables.
No performance obligation exists until technical support expires.
ref: Ind AS 115 (Revenue from Contracts with Customers) - Paragraphs 27-30: Distinct Goods or Services
explanation: Under Ind AS 115 Paragraph 29, a good or service is not distinct within the context of the contract if the entity provides a significant service of integrating the good or service with other goods or services into a bundle of goods or services that represent the combined output. Because the software is significantly modified and integrated, the license and customization are bundled into a single performance obligation. Technical support is distinct and forms a second performance obligation.

subject: Financial Reporting
tag: [ICAI CA Final FR PYQ] Ind AS 115: Variable Consideration & Constraint
question: InfraBuild Ltd. enters into a contract to build a municipal flyover for a fixed price of ₹100 Crores with completion due on 31st December 2024. The contract includes an incentive bonus of ₹10 Crores if completed by 30th November 2024. Historical analysis indicates a 75% probability of early completion. However, ongoing monsoon flooding and geotechnical approvals create significant uncertainty outside management's control. Under Ind AS 115, how should the variable consideration be estimated and recognized as of 31st March 2024?
options: Include the full ₹10 Crores incentive bonus in the transaction price based on the 75% probability.
Include ₹7.5 Crores (expected value: 75% of ₹10 Crores) in the transaction price.

Exclude the ₹10 Crores bonus from the transaction price under the 'variable consideration constraint', because it is not highly probable that a significant reversal in cumulative revenue will not occur once uncertainty is resolved.
Recognize the ₹10 Crores incentive in OCI.
ref: Ind AS 115 - Paragraphs 56-58: Constraining Estimates of Variable Consideration
explanation: Ind AS 115 Paragraph 56 states that an entity shall include in the transaction price some or all of an amount of variable consideration only to the extent that it is 'highly probable' that a significant reversal in the amount of cumulative revenue recognized will not occur when the uncertainty is subsequently resolved. Factors such as susceptibility to factors outside the entity's influence (weather, regulatory approvals) require the variable incentive to be fully constrained until resolution.

subject: Financial Reporting
tag: [ICAI CA Final FR PYQ] Ind AS 115: Significant Financing Component
question: Solar EPC Ltd. agrees to construct a solar power plant for CleanEnergy Ltd. for ₹121 Crores payable 2 years after plant commissioning and operational handover. The cash selling price of an equivalent plant paid upon handover is ₹100 Crores. The customer's market borrowing rate is 10% per annum. How should Solar EPC Ltd. account for this contract under Ind AS 115 upon handover and over the 2-year credit period?
options: Recognize revenue of ₹121 Crores on handover date; no financing income.

Recognize revenue of ₹100 Crores on handover date (the cash selling price/present value) and recognize finance income of ₹10 Crores in Year 1 (10% of ₹100 Cr) and ₹11 Crores in Year 2 (10% of ₹110 Cr) in Profit & Loss using the effective interest method.
Recognize revenue of ₹60.5 Crores in each of the two years.
Recognize revenue of ₹121 Crores only after cash is received at the end of year 2.
ref: Ind AS 115 - Paragraphs 60-65: Significant Financing Component in a Contract
explanation: Under Ind AS 115, when the contract contains a significant financing component, the transaction price is adjusted to reflect the time value of money. The entity recognizes revenue at the cash selling price of ₹100 Crores at the point when control of the plant is transferred. The ₹21 Crores difference is recognized as finance income over the 2-year deferred settlement period using the effective interest method.

subject: Financial Reporting
tag: [ICAI CA Final FR PYQ] Ind AS 115: Standalone Selling Price Allocation
question: Telecom Pioneer Ltd. sells a bundled mobile package comprising a high-end smartphone and a 12-month voice/data service contract for a total upfront consideration of ₹60,000. Standalone selling prices are: Smartphone = ₹48,000; 12-month service contract = ₹32,000 (Total standalone price = ₹80,000). How should the ₹60,000 transaction price be allocated to the performance obligations under Ind AS 115?
options: Allocate ₹48,000 to the smartphone upon delivery, and remaining ₹12,000 to the 12-month service contract.

Allocate pro-rata based on relative standalone selling prices: Smartphone = (₹48,000 / ₹80,000) × ₹60,000 = ₹36,000 recognized on delivery; Service = (₹32,000 / ₹80,000) × ₹60,000 = ₹24,000 recognized ratably over 12 months (₹2,000/month).
Split 50:50 (₹30,000 each) between the smartphone and service.
Recognize entire ₹60,000 on delivery of the smartphone.
ref: Ind AS 115 - Paragraphs 73-76: Allocation Based on Relative Standalone Selling Prices
explanation: Ind AS 115 Paragraph 73 states that an entity shall allocate the transaction price to each performance obligation on a relative standalone selling price basis. The total standalone price is ₹48,000 + ₹32,000 = ₹80,000. The discount of 25% (₹20,000 / ₹80,000) is allocated proportionately to both obligations: Phone = ₹48,000 × 75% = ₹36,000; Service = ₹32,000 × 75% = ₹24,000.

subject: Financial Reporting
tag: [ICAI CA Final FR PYQ] Ind AS 115: Input Method for Construction Contracts
question: MegaStructure Ltd. enters into a fixed-price construction contract for ₹500 Crores. Total estimated contract costs are ₹400 Crores. During Year 1, actual costs incurred were ₹100 Crores (which includes ₹20 Crores for specialized architectural steel delivered to site but not yet fabricated or installed). MegaStructure measures progress using the input method (costs incurred). What is the percentage of completion and revenue recognized in Year 1 under Ind AS 115?
options: Cost incurred ₹100 Cr / ₹400 Cr = 25%; Revenue = ₹125 Crores.

Uninstalled material (₹20 Cr) must be excluded from progress measurement. Incurred operational costs = ₹80 Cr; Total estimated costs = ₹400 Cr; Progress = ₹80 / ₹400 = 20%; Revenue recognized = 20% of ₹500 Cr = ₹100 Crores (or ₹80 Cr + ₹20 Cr uninstalled materials at zero profit).
Revenue recognized is zero until the building structure is finished.
Recognize revenue equal to customer billings of ₹150 Crores.
ref: Ind AS 115 - Paragraph B19: Uninstalled Materials Adjustment in Input Method
explanation: Under Ind AS 115 Paragraph B19, an entity shall exclude from an input measure of progress any costs incurred that do not contribute to the entity's progress in satisfying the performance obligation (such as uninstalled materials). When uninstalled materials are significant, the entity recognizes revenue only to the extent of the cost incurred for those materials with zero profit margin, or excludes them from the progress calculation.

subject: Financial Reporting
tag: [ICAI CA Final FR PYQ] Ind AS 115: Contract Modifications - Prospective vs Cumulative Catch-Up
question: BuildCon Ltd. has a contract to construct 100 identical prefabricated modular classrooms for a school district for ₹100 Crores (₹1 Crore each). After delivering 60 classrooms (revenue recognized ₹60 Crores), the client requests 20 additional classrooms. The price for the additional 20 classrooms is negotiated at ₹80 Lakhs each, which does NOT reflect their standalone selling price. How should this contract modification be accounted for under Ind AS 115?
options: As a separate contract.

As a termination of the existing contract and creation of a new contract (prospective treatment), because the remaining 40 original classrooms and 20 new classrooms are distinct, but the additional price does not reflect standalone selling price; total remaining consideration of ₹56 Crores (₹40 Cr + ₹16 Cr) is allocated over 60 remaining classrooms at ₹93.33 Lakhs each.
As a cumulative catch-up adjustment against already recognized revenue of ₹60 Crores.
Revenue for the 20 new classrooms must be deferred until all 120 are completed.
ref: Ind AS 115 - Paragraph 21(a): Contract Modification as Prospective Replacement
explanation: Under Ind AS 115 Paragraph 21(a), an entity accounts for a contract modification as if it were a termination of the existing contract and the creation of a new contract if the remaining goods are distinct from those transferred on or before the modification date, but the additional goods are not priced at their standalone selling prices. The remaining consideration (₹40 Cr + ₹16 Cr = ₹56 Cr) is allocated prospectively to the 60 remaining distinct classrooms.

subject: Financial Reporting
tag: [ICAI CA Final FR PYQ] Ind AS 115: Principal vs Agent Assessment
question: TicketFlyer Ltd. operates an online portal for airline bookings. The portal displays flights, processes passenger payments of ₹10,000 per ticket, remits ₹9,200 to the airline, and retains an ₹800 commission. TicketFlyer does not control the seat inventory before transfer, does not set flight schedules, and bears no inventory or flight operational risk. How should TicketFlyer Ltd. recognize revenue under Ind AS 115?
options: Recognize gross revenue of ₹10,000 and cost of sales of ₹9,200 as a Principal.
Recognize net revenue of ₹800 as an Agent, because TicketFlyer does not obtain control of the flight service before it is transferred to the customer.
Recognize no revenue until the passenger completes the flight.
Recognize ₹10,000 in Other Comprehensive Income.
ref: Ind AS 115 - Paragraphs B34-B38: Principal versus Agent Considerations
explanation: Ind AS 115 Paragraph B34 states that when another party is involved in providing goods or services to a customer, the entity must determine whether it is a principal (controlling the specified good or service before transfer) or an agent (arranging for the good or service to be provided by the other party). Because TicketFlyer does not control the service before it is provided, it is an agent and recognizes revenue net at ₹800.

subject: Financial Reporting
tag: [ICAI CA Final FR PYQ] Ind AS 115: Non-Refundable Upfront Fees
question: Club Royale charges new members an upfront non-refundable joining fee of ₹1,20,000 plus an annual membership fee of ₹24,000. The upfront fee does not transfer any distinct good or service to the member, but provides an ongoing right to access club amenities over an estimated average membership life of 5 years. How should the upfront fee be recognized under Ind AS 115?
options: Recognize full ₹1,20,000 as revenue immediately on receipt, because it is non-refundable.
Recognize the ₹1,20,000 upfront fee as a contract liability and amortize it as revenue ratably over the estimated 5-year customer relationship period (₹24,000 per year).
Credit the upfront fee directly to Equity Share Capital.
Recognize the upfront fee in OCI.
ref: Ind AS 115 - Paragraph B49: Non-Refundable Upfront Fees
explanation: Under Ind AS 115 Paragraph B49, non-refundable upfront fees (such as joining fees or setup fees) that do not transfer a distinct good or service to the customer are treated as an advance payment for future goods or services. Therefore, the fee is recognized as revenue over the period during which those future goods or services are expected to be provided (the expected customer relationship period).

subject: Financial Reporting
tag: [ICAI CA Final FR PYQ] Ind AS 115: Warranties - Assurance vs Service Type
question: ElectroTech Ltd. sells an industrial laser for ₹20 Lakhs. The purchase price includes: (i) a statutory 1-year warranty assuring that the laser complies with agreed specifications and is free from defects; and (ii) a customer option to purchase an additional 2-year extended preventative maintenance warranty for ₹2 Lakhs. How are these two warranties treated under Ind AS 115?
options: Both warranties are separate performance obligations requiring transaction price allocation.

The 1-year statutory warranty is an assurance-type warranty accounted for as a provision under Ind AS 37; the optional 2-year extended warranty is a service-type warranty that represents a distinct performance obligation, with revenue recognized over the 2-year service period.
Both warranties are accounted for under Ind AS 37.
All warranty proceeds are deferred until all 3 years expire.
ref: Ind AS 115 - Paragraphs B28-B33: Customer Warranties
explanation: Under Ind AS 115, if a customer does not have the option to purchase a warranty separately and the warranty only provides assurance that the product complies with agreed specifications, it is an assurance-type warranty accounted for under Ind AS 37. If the customer can purchase the warranty separately or it provides a service beyond basic assurance, it is a service-type warranty and accounted for as a separate performance obligation.

subject: Financial Reporting
tag: [ICAI CA Final FR PYQ] Ind AS 115: Performance Obligation Satisfied Over Time Criteria
question: Which of the following conditions mandates that a performance obligation is satisfied over time (rather than at a point in time) under Ind AS 115?
options: The contract price exceeds ₹100 Crores.

Any one of the following three criteria is met: (a) customer simultaneously receives and consumes benefits as entity performs; (b) entity's performance creates or enhances an asset customer controls; or (c) entity's performance does not create an asset with an alternative use to entity AND entity has an enforceable right to payment for performance completed to date.
The customer inspects the asset at the entity's premises prior to shipment.
The contract contains a penalty clause for delayed delivery.
ref: Ind AS 115 - Paragraph 35: Criteria for Satisfaction of Performance Obligations Over Time
explanation: Ind AS 115 Paragraph 35 defines three distinct criteria where control transfers over time: (a) simultaneous receipt and consumption (routine services); (b) asset created/enhanced under customer control (building on customer land); or (c) no alternative use to the entity and an enforceable right to payment for performance completed to date (custom asset with cost-plus-margin enforceable right).

subject: Financial Reporting
tag: [ICAI CA Final FR PYQ] Ind AS 115: Incremental Costs of Obtaining a Contract
question: RealEstate Developers Ltd. pays sales commission of ₹5 Lakhs to an external broker upon the successful signing of an enforceable apartment sale contract. The apartment will be constructed over 3 years. Additionally, the company incurred ₹1 Lakh on legal fees drafting standard tender templates (incurred regardless of whether the contract was won). How should these costs be treated under Ind AS 115?
options: Expense both the ₹5 Lakhs commission and ₹1 Lakh legal fees immediately in Profit or Loss.

Capitalize the ₹5 Lakhs sales commission as an asset (incremental cost of obtaining a contract) and amortize it over the 3-year construction period; expense the ₹1 Lakh legal fees as incurred because they would have been incurred regardless of contract award.
Capitalize both costs into property inventory.
Deduct ₹6 Lakhs directly from equity.
ref: Ind AS 115 - Paragraphs 91-94: Incremental Costs of Obtaining a Contract
explanation: Under Ind AS 115 Paragraph 91, an entity shall recognize as an asset the incremental costs of obtaining a contract with a customer if the entity expects to recover those costs. Incremental costs are those that would not have been incurred if the contract had not been obtained (e.g. sales commission). Costs incurred regardless of whether the contract was obtained (like bid preparation and legal fees) are expensed as incurred.

subject: Financial Reporting
tag: [ICAI CA Final FR PYQ] Ind AS 115: Right of Return and Refund Liability
question: Fashion Trendz Ltd. sells 1,000 designer dresses at ₹5,000 each (cost ₹3,000 each) in March 2024. Customers have an unconditional 30-day right of return for full cash refund. Historical data establishes that 8% of dresses will be returned. As of 31st March 2024, how should this sale be recorded under Ind AS 115?
options: Recognize revenue of ₹50,00,000 and cost of sales of ₹30,00,000.

Recognize revenue of ₹46,00,000 (920 dresses), a refund liability of ₹4,00,000 (80 dresses × ₹5,000), cost of sales of ₹27,60,000 (920 dresses × ₹3,000), and an asset for recovery of products of ₹2,40,000 (80 dresses × ₹3,000).
Defer all revenue until the 30-day return window lapses.
Recognize revenue of ₹50,00,000 and a warranty provision of ₹4,00,000 under Ind AS 37.
ref: Ind AS 115 - Paragraphs B20-B27: Sale with a Right of Return
explanation: For sales with a right of return, an entity recognizes: (a) revenue for the transferred products in the amount of consideration to which the entity expects to be entitled (92% = ₹46L); (b) a refund liability for amounts expected to be refunded (8% = ₹4L); (c) cost of sales for goods expected not to be returned (92% = ₹27.6L); and (d) an asset for its right to recover products from customers on settling the refund liability (8% = ₹2.4L).

subject: Financial Reporting
tag: [ICAI CA Final FR PYQ] Ind AS 115: Licensing - Right to Access vs Right to Use
question: MovieMagic Studios grants a streaming platform a 3-year license to stream a finished 1995 blockbuster movie. The studio has no obligation to undertake any activities that significantly affect the intellectual property of the film. Is this license a 'Right to Access' (revenue over time) or a 'Right to Use' (revenue at point in time) under Ind AS 115?
options: Right to Access, recognized ratably over the 3-year streaming license window.

Right to Use, recognized in full at the point in time when the customer is able to use and benefit from the license (the effective commencement date), because the intellectual property has significant standalone functionality and the licensor undertakes no activities affecting it.
A financial lease under Ind AS 116.
Recognized based on viewer streaming hours only.
ref: Ind AS 115 - Paragraphs B56-B61: Licensing of Intellectual Property
explanation: Ind AS 115 distinguishes between: (a) a right to access IP (dynamic license where the licensor's ongoing activities significantly affect the IP, recognized over time); and (b) a right to use IP (static license where the IP has standalone functionality and the licensor's activities do not change it, recognized at the point in time when the license is transferred and operational).

subject: Financial Reporting
tag: [ICAI CA Final FR PYQ] Ind AS 115: Bill-and-Hold Arrangements
question: On 28th March 2024, Machinery Corp sells custom equipment to a client for ₹50 Lakhs. The client requests in writing that Machinery Corp retain physical custody in its warehouse until the client's new factory site is ready in May 2024. The equipment is complete, identified separately, ready for physical delivery, and cannot be redirected to any other customer. Can Machinery Corp recognize revenue in March 2024 under Ind AS 115?
options: No, revenue recognition is strictly prohibited until physical delivery occurs.

Yes, all four bill-and-hold criteria under Ind AS 115 Paragraph B81 are met (substantive reason for request, separately identified as customer's, ready for physical transfer, entity cannot use or redirect the product), allowing control to transfer and revenue to be recognized.
Only 50% revenue can be recognized.
Revenue is recognized under Ind AS 116 as a lease.
ref: Ind AS 115 - Paragraphs B79-B82: Bill-and-Hold Arrangements
explanation: Under Ind AS 115 Paragraph B81, for a customer to have obtained control in a bill-and-hold arrangement, all of the following criteria must be met: (a) reason for bill-and-hold must be substantive (customer requested); (b) product must be identified separately; (c) product must be ready for physical transfer; and (d) entity cannot have the ability to use the product or direct it to another customer.

subject: Financial Reporting
tag: [ICAI CA Final FR PYQ] Ind AS 115: Customer Options for Additional Goods (Material Right)
question: Retail Store Ltd. launches a customer loyalty program: for every ₹1,000 spent on groceries, the customer receives 10 reward points. Each point entitles the customer to a ₹10 discount on future purchases. Management expects 80% of points to be redeemed. During the month, customers spend ₹1,00,000 and earn 1,000 points (fair value of points expected to be redeemed = 800 × ₹10 = ₹8,000). How should the ₹1,00,000 transaction price be allocated under Ind AS 115?
options: Recognize full ₹1,00,000 as revenue immediately and provide for ₹8,000 as an expense under Ind AS 37.

Allocate the ₹1,00,000 consideration between the groceries delivered (₹1,00,000 / ₹1,08,000 × ₹1,00,000 = ₹92,593 recognized immediately) and the performance obligation for loyalty points (₹8,000 / ₹1,08,000 × ₹1,00,000 = ₹7,407 recognized as a contract liability until points are redeemed or expire).
Defer all revenue until points are redeemed.
Recognize points in OCI.
ref: Ind AS 115 - Paragraphs B39-B43: Customer Options for Additional Goods or Services (Loyalty Points)
explanation: If in a contract an entity grants a customer the option to acquire additional goods or services, that option gives rise to a performance obligation if the option provides a material right to the customer. The entity allocates the transaction price to the performance obligations on a relative standalone selling price basis. Revenue allocated to points is recognized as a contract liability until points are redeemed or expire.

subject: Financial Reporting
tag: [ICAI CA Final FR PYQ] Ind AS 115: Consignment Arrangements
question: Auto Components Ltd. ships 500 gearboxes to a nationwide dealer network. The agreement specifies that the dealer takes no inventory risk, Auto Components Ltd. may recall or transfer gearboxes to another dealer at any time, and the dealer has no obligation to pay until a gearbox is sold to an end consumer. How should Auto Components Ltd. recognize revenue?
options: Recognize revenue upon shipment of gearboxes to the dealer's warehouse.

No revenue is recognized upon shipment; revenue is recognized only when the dealer sells the gearbox to an end customer, because control remains with Auto Components Ltd. in a consignment arrangement.
Recognize revenue at 50% upon shipment and 50% upon final sale.
Recognize revenue under Ind AS 109 as a financial asset.
ref: Ind AS 115 - Paragraphs B77-B78: Consignment Arrangements
explanation: Under Ind AS 115 Paragraph B77, when an entity delivers a product to another party for sale to end customers, the entity must evaluate whether that other party has obtained control. In a consignment arrangement (where the entity controls the product until a specified event occurs, can require return or transfer, and dealer has no unconditional obligation to pay), revenue is not recognized on delivery to the dealer.

subject: Financial Reporting
tag: [ICAI CA Final FR PYQ] Ind AS 115: Onerous Contracts under Ind AS 115 / Ind AS 37
question: BridgeTech Ltd. is executing a fixed-price construction contract for ₹80 Crores. By the end of Year 1, costs incurred were ₹40 Crores and estimated costs to complete are ₹60 Crores (total expected costs = ₹100 Crores). Progress is 40% (₹40 Cr / ₹100 Cr). Revenue recognized to date is ₹32 Crores (40% of ₹80 Cr). How should the expected total contract loss of ₹20 Crores (₹80 Cr - ₹100 Cr) be treated under Ind AS 115 and Ind AS 37?
options: Recognize the ₹20 Crores loss ratably over the remaining construction period.

Recognize an immediate provision for the entire remaining onerous contract loss of ₹12 Crores in Profit & Loss (after reflecting the current period operating loss of ₹8 Crores: ₹32 Cr revenue minus ₹40 Cr costs), ensuring the entire ₹20 Crores expected contract loss is recognized immediately.
Capitalize the ₹20 Crores loss as an intangible asset.
Defer recognition of the loss until final handover.
ref: Ind AS 115 & Ind AS 37: Onerous Construction Contracts
explanation: When a construction contract becomes onerous (total contract costs exceed total contract revenues), the entire expected loss must be recognized immediately in profit or loss in accordance with Ind AS 37. Current year P&L reflects ₹32 Cr revenue - ₹40 Cr costs = -₹8 Cr loss, plus an onerous contract provision of ₹12 Cr = total ₹20 Cr recognized immediately.

subject: Financial Reporting
tag: [ICAI CA Final FR PYQ] Ind AS 115: Non-Cash Consideration Measurement
question: TechGlobal Ltd. agrees to develop an automated inventory management app for a corporate client. In exchange, the client transfers 1,00,000 equity shares of its own company to TechGlobal Ltd. The fair value of the shares at contract inception is ₹50 per share (₹50 Lakhs). At the date of app completion and handover, the share price has risen to ₹65 per share (₹65 Lakhs). Under Ind AS 115, at what amount is transaction revenue measured?
options: ₹65 Lakhs (fair value of non-cash consideration at the date of delivery).
₹50 Lakhs (measured at fair value of the non-cash consideration at contract inception).
₹10 Lakhs (nominal face value of shares).
Zero revenue; shares are treated as capital reserve.
ref: Ind AS 115 - Paragraphs 66-69: Measurement of Non-Cash Consideration
explanation: Under Ind AS 115 Paragraph 66, to determine the transaction price for contracts in which a customer promises consideration in a form other than cash, an entity shall measure the non-cash consideration at fair value. Under Ind AS guidance, fair value of non-cash consideration is measured at contract inception and subsequent changes in fair value due to the form of the consideration (share price fluctuation) are not recognized as revenue.

subject: Financial Reporting
tag: [ICAI CA Final FR PYQ] Ind AS 115: Contract Asset vs Trade Receivable
question: What is the fundamental distinction between a 'Contract Asset' and a 'Trade Receivable' under Ind AS 115?
options: There is no distinction; both terms are interchangeable.

A Trade Receivable represents an unconditional right to consideration (only the passage of time is required before payment is due), whereas a Contract Asset represents an entity's right to consideration in exchange for goods/services transferred to the customer conditioned on something other than the passage of time (e.g. future performance or milestone certification).
A Contract Asset is always classified as Non-Current, while a Trade Receivable is Current.
Contract Assets carry no credit risk, while Trade Receivables do.
ref: Ind AS 115 - Paragraphs 107-108: Contract Asset vs Trade Receivable
explanation: Ind AS 115 Paragraph 107 states that an entity shall present a contract asset when it has performed by transferring goods or services before the customer pays consideration, conditioned on something other than the passage of time. A receivable is an entity's right to consideration that is unconditional—only the passage of time is required before payment becomes due.

subject: Financial Reporting
tag: [ICAI CA Final FR PYQ] Ind AS 115: Presentation of Contract Liabilities
question: SmartTech Ltd. receives an advance payment of ₹25 Crores from a client on 15th March 2024 for specialized industrial robotics to be manufactured and delivered in November 2024. As of 31st March 2024, manufacturing has not commenced. How must the ₹25 Crores be presented on SmartTech Ltd.'s balance sheet?
options: Revenue in the Statement of Profit and Loss for FY 2023-24.
Contract Liability (Deferred Revenue) under Current Liabilities, representing the entity's obligation to transfer goods to the customer for which consideration has been received.
Other Comprehensive Income.
Deduction from Inventory.
ref: Ind AS 115 - Paragraph 106: Presentation of Contract Liabilities
explanation: Ind AS 115 Paragraph 106 states: 'If a customer pays consideration, or an entity has a right to an amount of consideration that is unconditional, before the entity transfers a good or service to the customer, the entity shall present the contract as a contract liability when the payment is made or the payment is due (whichever is earlier).' A contract liability is an entity's obligation to transfer goods or services.

subject: Financial Reporting
topicTitle: Leases, Employee Benefits, Share-Based Payments, and Income Taxes
tag: [ICAI CA Final FR PYQ] Ind AS 116: Initial Measurement of Lease Liability & ROU Asset
question: On 1st April 2023, Retail Hub Ltd. enters into a 5-year lease for commercial space with annual lease payments of ₹20,00,000 payable at the end of each financial year. The lessee's incremental borrowing rate is 10% per annum (Cumulative PV Factor for 5 years at 10% = 3.7908). Retail Hub Ltd. incurs initial direct costs of ₹2,00,000, receives a lease incentive of ₹1,00,000 from the lessor, and estimates site restoration costs of ₹3,00,000 (present value at 10% = ₹1,86,300). What are the initial carrying amounts of the Lease Liability and the Right-of-Use (ROU) Asset on 1st April 2023?
options: Lease Liability = ₹1,00,00,000; ROU Asset = ₹1,00,00,000.

Lease Liability = ₹75,81,600 (PV of lease payments); ROU Asset = ₹78,67,900 (Lease liability ₹75,81,600 + Initial direct costs ₹2,00,000 - Lease incentive ₹1,00,000 + PV of restoration obligation ₹1,86,300).
Lease Liability = ₹75,81,600; ROU Asset = ₹75,81,600.
Lease Liability = ₹78,67,900; ROU Asset = ₹80,00,000.
ref: Ind AS 116 (Leases) - Paragraphs 23-28: Initial Measurement of ROU Asset & Lease Liability
explanation: Under Ind AS 116 Paragraph 26, the lease liability is measured at the present value of the lease payments that are not paid at the commencement date (₹20,00,000 × 3.7908 = ₹75,81,600). Under Paragraph 24, the cost of the ROU asset comprises: (a) initial measurement of lease liability (₹75,81,600); (b) lease payments made at or before commencement date less lease incentives received (-₹1,00,000); (c) initial direct costs incurred (₹2,00,000); and (d) estimated dismantling/restoration costs (₹1,86,300). Total ROU Asset = ₹78,67,900.

subject: Financial Reporting
topicTitle: Leases, Employee Benefits, Share-Based Payments, and Income Taxes
tag: [ICAI CA Final FR PYQ] Ind AS 116: Sale and Leaseback Transaction
question: Apex Logistics Ltd. sells its warehouse (carrying amount ₹40 Crores, fair value ₹60 Crores) to an institutional buyer for ₹60 Crores cash, and simultaneously leases it back for 10 years at market rental. The transfer of the warehouse qualifies as a sale under Ind AS 115. The present value of the annual lease payments is ₹20 Crores. What is the initial carrying amount of the ROU Asset retained by Apex Logistics and the gain on sale recognized in Profit or Loss under Ind AS 116?
options: ROU Asset = ₹20 Crores; Gain on sale = ₹20 Crores.

ROU Asset = ₹13.33 Crores (Carrying amount ₹40 Cr × PV of leaseback ₹20 Cr / Fair value ₹60 Cr); Gain on sale recognized in P&L = ₹13.33 Crores (Total gain ₹20 Cr × Proportion relating to rights transferred: (₹60 Cr - ₹20 Cr) / ₹60 Cr = 66.67%).
ROU Asset = ₹40 Crores; Gain on sale = Nil.
ROU Asset = ₹60 Crores; Gain on sale = ₹20 Crores.
ref: Ind AS 116 - Paragraphs 98-102: Sale and Leaseback Transactions
explanation: Under Ind AS 116 Paragraph 100, if the transfer of an asset by the seller-lessee satisfies the requirements of Ind AS 115 to be accounted for as a sale, the seller-lessee shall measure the ROU asset arising from the leaseback at the proportion of the previous carrying amount of the asset that relates to the right of use retained by the seller-lessee: ₹40 Cr × (₹20 Cr / ₹60 Cr) = ₹13.33 Crores. The seller-lessee recognizes only the amount of any gain or loss that relates to the rights transferred to the buyer-lessor: (₹60 Cr - ₹40 Cr) × [(₹60 Cr - ₹20 Cr) / ₹60 Cr] = ₹20 Cr × 2/3 = ₹13.33 Crores in P&L.

subject: Financial Reporting
topicTitle: Leases, Employee Benefits, Share-Based Payments, and Income Taxes
tag: [ICAI CA Final FR PYQ] Ind AS 19: Defined Benefit Plans - Actuarial Gains and Losses
question: During FY 2023-24, Zenith Ltd. obtained an actuarial valuation for its employee gratuity scheme under Ind AS 19. The valuation showed: Current Service Cost = ₹15 Crores; Net Interest Expense on Defined Benefit Liability = ₹5 Crores; Past Service Cost arising from plan amendment = ₹3 Crores; and Actuarial Loss arising from changes in demographic and financial assumptions = ₹8 Crores. Where should these components be recognized?
options: All ₹31 Crores must be recognized in the Statement of Profit and Loss.

Service cost (₹15 Cr Current + ₹3 Cr Past = ₹18 Cr) and Net Interest (₹5 Cr) totaling ₹23 Crores are recognized in Profit and Loss; the Actuarial Loss of ₹8 Crores (remeasurement) is recognized in Other Comprehensive Income (OCI) and cannot be reclassified to profit or loss in subsequent periods.
All ₹31 Crores must be recognized in Other Comprehensive Income.
Actuarial loss is amortized over the remaining average service life using the corridor approach.
ref: Ind AS 19 (Employee Benefits) - Paragraphs 57, 120-122: Remeasurements in OCI
explanation: Ind AS 19 Paragraph 120 mandates that an entity shall recognize the components of defined benefit cost as follows: (a) service cost (current service cost, past service cost, and gain/loss on settlement) in profit or loss; (b) net interest on the net defined benefit liability (asset) in profit or loss; and (c) remeasurements (actuarial gains and losses, return on plan assets excluding amounts in net interest) in Other Comprehensive Income. Remeasurements recognized in OCI shall not be reclassified to profit or loss.

subject: Financial Reporting
topicTitle: Leases, Employee Benefits, Share-Based Payments, and Income Taxes
tag: [ICAI CA Final FR PYQ] Ind AS 19: Projected Unit Credit Method
question: Which actuarial valuation method is mandatorily required under Ind AS 19 to determine the present value of defined benefit obligations and the related current service cost?
options: Entry Age Normal Method.
Projected Unit Credit (PUC) Method (sometimes known as the accrued benefit method prorated on service or as the benefit/years of service method).
Attained Age Normal Method.
Aggregate Cost Method.
ref: Ind AS 19 - Paragraph 67: Projected Unit Credit Method
explanation: Ind AS 19 Paragraph 67 states explicitly: 'An entity shall use the projected unit credit method to determine the present value of its defined benefit obligations and the related current service cost and, where applicable, past service cost.' This method sees each period of service as giving rise to an additional unit of benefit entitlement and measures each unit separately.

subject: Financial Reporting
topicTitle: Leases, Employee Benefits, Share-Based Payments, and Income Taxes
tag: [ICAI CA Final FR PYQ] Ind AS 102: Equity-Settled vs Cash-Settled Share-Based Payments
question: What is the fundamental difference in measurement and balance sheet presentation between an Equity-Settled Share-Based Payment (e.g. ESOP) and a Cash-Settled Share-Based Payment (e.g. Share Appreciation Rights - SARs) under Ind AS 102?
options: Equity-settled awards are measured at fair value on each reporting date and presented as liabilities; cash-settled awards are measured at grant date and presented in equity.

Equity-settled awards are measured at fair value at grant date and recognized in equity without subsequent remeasurement for share price changes; cash-settled awards are measured at fair value at each reporting date until settlement, with changes in fair value recognized in profit or loss and presented as a financial liability.
Both are recognized strictly when shares or cash are physically distributed to employees.
Cash-settled awards are expensed only if market conditions are satisfied.
ref: Ind AS 102 (Share-based Payment) - Paragraphs 10-13 & 30-33
explanation: Under Ind AS 102, for equity-settled transactions, the fair value of goods or services received is measured by reference to the fair value of equity instruments granted at grant date, credited to Equity, and never subsequently remeasured for changes in market prices. For cash-settled transactions, the entity measures the goods or services acquired and the liability incurred at the fair value of the liability at each reporting date until settlement, with changes in fair value recognized in profit or loss.

subject: Financial Reporting
topicTitle: Leases, Employee Benefits, Share-Based Payments, and Income Taxes
tag: [ICAI CA Final FR PYQ] Ind AS 102: Non-Market vs Market Performance Conditions
question: On 1st April 2023, TechNova Ltd. grants 10,000 share options to its VP. The options vest in 3 years provided: (Condition A) company EPS grows by 12% per annum (non-market condition); and (Condition B) company stock price reaches ₹500 on the National Stock Exchange (market condition). How are market and non-market vesting conditions factored into accounting under Ind AS 102?
options: Both conditions are ignored until the 3-year vesting date arrives.

Market conditions (stock price target) are taken into account when estimating the grant-date fair value of the options and are not subsequently adjusted whether the condition is met or not; non-market conditions (EPS growth) are NOT taken into account in estimating grant-date fair value, but are taken into account by adjusting the number of equity instruments expected to vest.
Non-market conditions are factored into fair value, while market conditions are adjusted in number of options.
If the market condition fails, all previously recognized compensation expense is reversed.
ref: Ind AS 102 - Paragraphs 19-21: Market and Non-Market Vesting Conditions
explanation: Under Ind AS 102 Paragraph 19, vesting conditions other than market conditions (such as service conditions and performance conditions like EPS/profit targets) shall not be taken into account when estimating the fair value of the shares or options at the measurement date. Instead, they are taken into account by adjusting the number of equity instruments included in the measurement. Under Paragraph 21, market conditions (such as a target share price) shall be taken into account when estimating the fair value of the equity instruments granted.

subject: Financial Reporting
topicTitle: Leases, Employee Benefits, Share-Based Payments, and Income Taxes
tag: [ICAI CA Final FR PYQ] Ind AS 12: Tax Base of Depreciable Asset & Temporary Difference
question: On 1st April 2023, Bharat Forgings Ltd. acquired machinery for ₹100 Crores. For financial accounting, the machinery is depreciated over 5 years on a straight-line basis (depreciation ₹20 Crores/year). For income tax purposes, tax depreciation is 30% on written down value (tax depreciation ₹30 Crores for Year 1). The applicable income tax rate is 25%. What is the deferred tax position as of 31st March 2024 under Ind AS 12?
options: Carrying amount = ₹80 Cr; Tax base = ₹70 Cr; Taxable temporary difference = ₹10 Cr; Deferred Tax Liability (DTL) = ₹2.5 Crores.
Carrying amount = ₹80 Cr; Tax base = ₹70 Cr; Deductible temporary difference = ₹10 Cr; Deferred Tax Asset (DTA) = ₹2.5 Crores.
No deferred tax arises because both books and tax will eventually equalize.
Deferred Tax Liability = ₹10 Crores.
ref: Ind AS 12 (Income Taxes) - Paragraphs 5-15: Taxable Temporary Differences and DTL
explanation: Carrying amount of machine in financial statements = ₹100 Cr - ₹20 Cr = ₹80 Crores. Tax base of machine (amount deductible for tax purposes in future periods) = ₹100 Cr - ₹30 Cr = ₹70 Crores. Because carrying amount exceeds tax base (₹80 Cr > ₹70 Cr), it gives rise to a taxable temporary difference of ₹10 Crores. Deferred Tax Liability = ₹10 Crores × 25% = ₹2.5 Crores recognized in Profit or Loss as deferred tax expense.

subject: Financial Reporting
topicTitle: Leases, Employee Benefits, Share-Based Payments, and Income Taxes
tag: [ICAI CA Final FR PYQ] Ind AS 12: Unused Tax Losses and Recognition of DTA
question: SolarTech Ltd. incurred an operating tax loss of ₹40 Crores in FY 2023-24 which can be carried forward for 8 years under the Income Tax Act. Management forecasts show that due to guaranteed power purchase agreements (PPAs), future taxable profits of ₹60 Crores are probable over the next 3 years against which the losses can be utilized. Applicable tax rate is 30%. Under Ind AS 12, can a Deferred Tax Asset (DTA) be recognized?
options: No, DTA can never be recognized on unused tax losses under Ind AS.

Yes, a Deferred Tax Asset of ₹12 Crores (₹40 Crores × 30%) should be recognized to the extent that it is probable that future taxable profit will be available against which the unused tax losses can be utilized.
A DTA of ₹18 Crores (₹60 Crores × 30%) should be recognized.
The tax loss must be recognized directly in OCI.
ref: Ind AS 12 - Paragraphs 34-36: Recognition of Deferred Tax Assets for Unused Tax Losses
explanation: Ind AS 12 Paragraph 34 states: 'A deferred tax asset shall be recognized for the carryforward of unused tax losses and unused tax credits to the extent that it is probable that future taxable profit will be available against which the unused tax losses and unused tax credits can be utilized.' Here, probable future taxable profits of ₹60 Cr easily absorb the ₹40 Cr loss; hence full DTA of ₹40 Cr × 30% = ₹12 Crores is recognized.

subject: Financial Reporting
topicTitle: Leases, Employee Benefits, Share-Based Payments, and Income Taxes
tag: [ICAI CA Final FR PYQ] Ind AS 116: Short-Term Lease & Low-Value Asset Exemptions
question: Which of the following leases qualifies for the optional recognition exemption under Ind AS 116, permitting the lessee to recognize lease payments as an operating expense on a straight-line basis without recognizing an ROU Asset and Lease Liability?
options: A 5-year lease of commercial headquarters building.
A 9-month lease of heavy earthmoving machinery with an option to purchase at an attractive price which the lessee is reasonably certain to exercise.
A 10-month lease of warehouse space with no purchase option (short-term lease) or a lease of IT tablets/laptops with brand-new value under ₹3.5 Lakhs (low-value assets).
A 3-year vehicle fleet lease.
ref: Ind AS 116 - Paragraphs 5-8: Recognition Exemptions for Leases
explanation: Under Ind AS 116 Paragraph 5, a lessee may elect not to apply the standard ROU model to: (a) short-term leases (lease term of 12 months or less and containing no purchase option); and (b) leases for which the underlying asset is of low value (e.g. personal computers, office furniture). If an entity elects either exemption, lease payments are recognized as an expense on either a straight-line basis over the lease term or another systematic basis.

subject: Financial Reporting
topicTitle: Leases, Employee Benefits, Share-Based Payments, and Income Taxes
tag: [ICAI CA Final FR PYQ] Ind AS 12: Substantively Enacted Tax Rates
question: On 31st March 2024, the prevailing corporate income tax rate is 30%. On 15th March 2024, the Parliament passed the Finance Act 2024, which received Presidential assent on 28th March 2024, lowering the tax rate to 25% effective for all future tax years beginning 1st April 2024. At what tax rate should temporary differences existing on 31st March 2024 be measured for deferred tax under Ind AS 12?
options: 30%, because the 30% rate applied throughout the financial year 2023-24.

25%, because deferred tax assets and liabilities are measured at the tax rates that are expected to apply to the period when the asset is realized or the liability is settled, based on tax rates (and tax laws) that have been enacted or substantively enacted by the end of the reporting period.
Average rate of 27.5%.
Deferred tax should not be recognized until 1st April 2024.
ref: Ind AS 12 - Paragraph 47: Measurement of Deferred Tax at Enacted Tax Rates
explanation: Ind AS 12 Paragraph 47 specifies: 'Deferred tax assets and liabilities shall be measured at the tax rates that are expected to apply to the period when the asset is realized or the liability is settled, based on tax rates (and tax laws) that have been enacted or substantively enacted by the end of the reporting period.' Because the 25% rate was enacted by 31st March 2024 for future periods when temporary differences reverse, it must be used.

subject: Financial Reporting
topicTitle: Leases, Employee Benefits, Share-Based Payments, and Income Taxes
tag: [ICAI CA Final FR PYQ] Ind AS 116: Lease Modification Decreasing Scope
question: A lessee leases 2,000 sq. meters of office space for 10 years. In Year 6, the lessee and lessor agree to amend the contract to reduce the leased space to 1,000 sq. meters (50% reduction in scope) and proportionately reduce lease payments. How does the lessee account for this lease modification under Ind AS 116?
options: Account for it as a brand-new separate lease.

Decrease the carrying amounts of both the ROU asset and lease liability by 50% to reflect the partial termination, and recognize any resulting difference as a gain or loss in Profit or Loss; then remeasure the remaining lease liability using a revised discount rate at the effective modification date with a corresponding adjustment to the remaining ROU asset.
Recognize the entire remaining ROU asset as an impairment loss.
No accounting entry is made until the end of year 10.
ref: Ind AS 116 - Paragraph 45: Lease Modification Decreasing the Scope of a Lease
explanation: Under Ind AS 116 Paragraph 45, for a lease modification that decreases the scope of a lease, the lessee shall decrease the carrying amount of the right-of-use asset to reflect the partial or full termination of the lease, and recognize in profit or loss any gain or loss relating to the partial or full termination. The remaining lease liability is then remeasured using a revised discount rate with an adjustment to the ROU asset.

subject: Financial Reporting
topicTitle: Leases, Employee Benefits, Share-Based Payments, and Income Taxes
tag: [ICAI CA Final FR PYQ] Ind AS 19: Past Service Cost Recognition
question: On 1st October 2023, Delta Ltd. improved its retirement pension plan by increasing employee pension multipliers retroactively for past service completed prior to 1st October 2023. The present value of the resulting increase in defined benefit obligation for unvested benefits is ₹10 Crores (vesting period 5 years), and for vested benefits is ₹15 Crores. How must Delta Ltd. recognize this past service cost under Ind AS 19?
options: Expense ₹15 Crores (vested) immediately and amortize ₹10 Crores (unvested) over 5 years.

Recognize the entire ₹25 Crores (both vested and unvested past service costs) immediately as an expense in Profit or Loss at the earlier of when the plan amendment occurs and when the entity recognizes related restructuring costs.
Amortize all ₹25 Crores over the remaining working life of employees.
Recognize all ₹25 Crores in Other Comprehensive Income.
ref: Ind AS 19 - Paragraphs 102-103: Immediate Recognition of Past Service Cost
explanation: Under Ind AS 19, past service cost (whether vested or unvested) must be recognized as an expense in profit or loss at the earlier of: (a) when the plan amendment or curtailment occurs; and (b) when the entity recognizes related restructuring costs under Ind AS 37 or termination benefits. Amortization of unvested past service cost is completely prohibited.

subject: Financial Reporting
topicTitle: Leases, Employee Benefits, Share-Based Payments, and Income Taxes
tag: [ICAI CA Final FR PYQ] Ind AS 102: Cancellation and Settlement of Share Options
question: During FY 2023-24, an entity cancels 5,000 equity-settled share options previously granted to directors (remaining unamortized grant-date fair value is ₹12 Lakhs). In compensation for the cancellation, the entity pays ₹15 Lakhs cash to the directors. The fair value of the options at the cancellation date was ₹14 Lakhs. How should this cancellation and cash settlement be accounted for under Ind AS 102?
options: Expense ₹15 Lakhs in P&L and credit Retained Earnings ₹12 Lakhs.

Account for the cancellation as an acceleration of vesting: immediately recognize the remaining unamortized grant-date fair value of ₹12 Lakhs in Profit & Loss; the cash payment up to the cancellation-date fair value of ₹14 Lakhs is treated as a repurchase of an equity interest (deducted from equity), while the excess ₹1 Lakh (₹15L - ₹14L) is recognized as an additional expense in Profit & Loss.
Credit ₹15 Lakhs to Share Capital.
Reverse all past compensation expense recognized in prior years.
ref: Ind AS 102 - Paragraph 28: Cancellations and Settlements of Equity-Settled Awards
explanation: Ind AS 102 Paragraph 28 states that if a grant of equity instruments is cancelled or settled during the vesting period: (a) the entity shall account for the cancellation or settlement as an acceleration of vesting, recognizing immediately the amount that otherwise would have been recognized for services over the remainder of the vesting period; and (b) any payment made shall be accounted for as the repurchase of an equity interest (deducted from equity), except that the extent that the payment exceeds the fair value of the equity instruments at repurchase date shall be recognized as an expense.

subject: Financial Reporting
topicTitle: Leases, Employee Benefits, Share-Based Payments, and Income Taxes
tag: [ICAI CA Final FR PYQ] Ind AS 12: Initial Recognition Exemption
question: Under Ind AS 12, when is an entity prohibited from recognizing a deferred tax asset or liability on the initial recognition of an asset or liability (the 'Initial Recognition Exemption')?
options: Whenever the asset is acquired using borrowed funds.

In a transaction that: (1) is not a business combination; (2) at the time of the transaction, affects neither accounting profit nor taxable profit (tax loss); and (3) does not give rise to equal taxable and deductible temporary differences at the time of the transaction.
Only for transactions involving foreign currency exchange.
Whenever the applicable tax rate is zero.
ref: Ind AS 12 - Paragraphs 15 & 24: Initial Recognition Exemption
explanation: Ind AS 12 prohibits recognizing a DTL/DTA on the initial recognition of an asset or liability in a transaction which: (a) is not a business combination; (b) at the time of the transaction, affects neither accounting profit nor taxable profit; and (c) at the time of the transaction, does not give rise to equal taxable and deductible temporary differences (narrow-scope amendment for leases and decommissioning).

subject: Financial Reporting
topicTitle: Leases, Employee Benefits, Share-Based Payments, and Income Taxes
tag: [ICAI CA Final FR PYQ] Ind AS 116: Variable Lease Payments Dependent on an Index vs Sales
question: A retail chain leases an anchor shop in a mall. The lease agreement requires: (i) an annual base rental of ₹50 Lakhs adjusted annually for changes in the Consumer Price Index (CPI); and (ii) a turnover rent equal to 3% of the shop's monthly gross sales revenue. How are these two variable payments included in the initial measurement of the Lease Liability under Ind AS 116?
options: Both variable payments must be estimated based on 5-year sales and inflation forecasts and capitalized into the lease liability.

Only variable lease payments that depend on an index or a rate (the CPI-linked base rent, measured using the index at commencement date) are included in the lease liability; variable payments based on sales/turnover are excluded from the lease liability and recognized as an expense in Profit or Loss in the period in which the triggering event or condition occurs.
Both are excluded from the lease liability.
Turnover rent is recognized in OCI.
ref: Ind AS 116 - Paragraphs 27(b) & 38: Variable Lease Payments
explanation: Ind AS 116 Paragraph 27(b) specifies that lease payments included in the measurement of the lease liability comprise variable lease payments that depend on an index or a rate, initially measured using the index or rate as at the commencement date. Variable lease payments linked to future sales or usage do not meet the definition of a liability until the sales occur, and are expensed in profit or loss as incurred.

subject: Financial Reporting
topicTitle: Leases, Employee Benefits, Share-Based Payments, and Income Taxes
tag: [ICAI CA Final FR PYQ] Ind AS 19: Asset Ceiling in Defined Benefit Plans
question: On 31st March 2024, an entity's defined benefit plan has plan assets with a fair value of ₹120 Crores and a present value of defined benefit obligation of ₹90 Crores (gross surplus = ₹30 Crores). The present value of available future refunds from the plan plus reductions in future employer contributions is ₹18 Crores (the asset ceiling). Under Ind AS 19, what net defined benefit asset should be presented on the balance sheet?
options: ₹30 Crores (full gross surplus).

₹18 Crores (net defined benefit asset is measured at the lower of the surplus in the defined benefit plan ₹30 Cr and the asset ceiling ₹18 Cr; the ₹12 Cr excess is recognized in OCI as an effect of the asset ceiling).
₹0, defined benefit assets are never recognized.
₹108 Crores.
ref: Ind AS 19 - Paragraph 64: Asset Ceiling for Defined Benefit Asset
explanation: Under Ind AS 19 Paragraph 64, when an entity has a surplus in a defined benefit plan, it shall measure the net defined benefit asset at the lower of: (a) the surplus in the defined benefit plan; and (b) the asset ceiling, determined using the discount rate. Any reduction in the net asset due to the asset ceiling is recognized in Other Comprehensive Income.

subject: Financial Reporting
topicTitle: Leases, Employee Benefits, Share-Based Payments, and Income Taxes
tag: [ICAI CA Final FR PYQ] Ind AS 102: Graded Vesting Attribution
question: On 1st April 2023, an entity grants 90,000 share options to its managers. The grant vests in three equal tranches: 30,000 options after 1 year, 30,000 options after 2 years, and 30,000 options after 3 years. Under Ind AS 102, can the entity recognize the total compensation expense straight-line over the full 3-year period?
options: Yes, straight-line spreading over the maximum 3-year term is mandatory.

No, Ind AS 102 explicitly mandates that each tranche must be treated as a separate share option grant with its own distinct vesting period and fair value; compensation expense for each tranche must be recognized separately over its respective service period (graded vesting attribution).
Yes, provided it is disclosed in the Director's Report.
Expense is recognized only when the third tranche vests.
ref: Ind AS 102 - Paragraphs 15 & IG11: Graded Vesting Schedule
explanation: Under Ind AS 102, where options vest in tranches (graded vesting), each tranche must be treated as a separate share-based payment award because each tranche has a different vesting period (1 year, 2 years, 3 years). An entity cannot treat the entire award as a single grant and spread the expense on a straight-line basis over 3 years; front-loaded graded vesting attribution is mandatory.

subject: Financial Reporting
topicTitle: Leases, Employee Benefits, Share-Based Payments, and Income Taxes
tag: [ICAI CA Final FR PYQ] Ind AS 12: Business Combinations & Deferred Taxes
question: Acquirer Ltd. acquires 100% of Target Ltd. in a business combination. In the purchase price allocation under Ind AS 103, an item of brand name is recognized at fair value of ₹50 Crores. For tax purposes, the tax base of the brand name is Nil (tax deductions are not available for brand amortization). Applicable tax rate is 30%. How should the deferred tax on this brand name be accounted for at acquisition date?
options: Recognize a Deferred Tax Liability of ₹15 Crores (₹50 Cr × 30%) with a corresponding debit to Profit or Loss.

Recognize a Deferred Tax Liability of ₹15 Crores (₹50 Cr × 30%) with a corresponding debit to Goodwill (or credit to capital reserve) in the business combination accounting, because the initial recognition exemption does NOT apply to business combinations.
No deferred tax is recognized under the initial recognition exemption.
Recognize a Deferred Tax Asset of ₹15 Crores.
ref: Ind AS 12 - Paragraphs 19 & 66: Deferred Taxes in Business Combinations
explanation: Ind AS 12 Paragraph 19 states that taxable temporary differences arise in a business combination when the fair values of identifiable assets acquired exceed their tax bases. Because the initial recognition exemption explicitly excludes business combinations, the entity recognizes a Deferred Tax Liability of ₹15 Crores with a corresponding increase to Goodwill (or reduction of bargain purchase gain).

subject: Financial Reporting
topicTitle: Leases, Employee Benefits, Share-Based Payments, and Income Taxes
tag: [ICAI CA Final FR PYQ] Ind AS 116: Sublease Classification by Intermediate Lessor
question: Prime Properties Ltd. leases a commercial floor for 10 years (head lease). 2 years later, Prime Properties subleases the exact same floor to another corporate tenant for the remaining 8 years of the head lease. How should Prime Properties Ltd. (as the intermediate lessor) classify the sublease under Ind AS 116?
options: By reference to the underlying physical real estate property (which has an economic life of 60 years).

By reference to the Right-of-Use (ROU) asset arising from the head lease (not by reference to the underlying physical asset); since the 8-year sublease is for the entire remaining term of the ROU asset, it is classified as a Finance Sublease, resulting in derecognition of the ROU asset and recognition of a Lease Receivable.
Always as an operating lease.
As an investment in property.
ref: Ind AS 116 - Paragraph B58: Sublease Classification by Intermediate Lessor
explanation: Under Ind AS 116 Paragraph B58, in classifying a sublease, an intermediate lessor shall classify the sublease as a finance lease or an operating lease by reference to the right-of-use asset arising from the head lease, rather than by reference to the underlying asset. Because the sublease covers the major part (100% of the remaining 8 years) of the ROU asset's life, it is a finance lease.

subject: Financial Reporting
topicTitle: Leases, Employee Benefits, Share-Based Payments, and Income Taxes
tag: [ICAI CA Final FR PYQ] Ind AS 12: Current vs Non-Current Presentation of Deferred Taxes
question: How does Ind AS 1 mandate the presentation of Deferred Tax Assets and Deferred Tax Liabilities on the Balance Sheet?
options: They must be bifurcated into Current and Non-Current portions based on expected reversal within 12 months.

An entity shall NOT classify deferred tax assets (or deferred tax liabilities) as current assets (or current liabilities); they must always be presented as Non-Current Assets or Non-Current Liabilities.
They must be presented under Cash and Cash Equivalents.
They must be presented in the Statement of Changes in Equity.
ref: Ind AS 1 - Paragraph 56: Mandatory Non-Current Presentation of Deferred Taxes
explanation: Ind AS 1 Paragraph 56 states unequivocally: 'When an entity presents current and non-current assets, and current and non-current liabilities, as separate classifications in its balance sheet, it shall not classify deferred tax assets (liabilities) as current assets (liabilities).' Deferred tax assets and liabilities are strictly classified as non-current.

subject: Financial Reporting
topicTitle: Provisions, Contingent Liabilities, and Events After the Reporting Period
tag: [ICAI CA Final FR PYQ] Ind AS 37: Restructuring Provision Criteria
question: On 15th December 2023, the Board of Directors of AutoParts Ltd. resolved to shut down its unprofitable brake-shoe manufacturing division. Prior to 31st March 2024, the company prepared a detailed formal restructuring plan, identified the locations and affected 400 employees, and sent individual redundancy and termination letters to employees with severance compensation terms. How should this restructuring be accounted for in the financial statements for the year ended 31st March 2024?
options: Disclose strictly as a contingent liability in the notes, because no severance cash has been disbursed before year-end.

Recognize a restructuring provision on 31st March 2024 for the direct expenditures arising from the restructuring (e.g. employee severance compensation), because the detailed formal plan and communication to affected employees created a valid constructive obligation.
Recognize a provision for both employee severance and anticipated future operating losses until complete closure.
No provision or disclosure is permitted until operations cease.
ref: Ind AS 37 (Provisions, Contingent Liabilities and Contingent Assets) - Paragraphs 70-83: Restructuring Provisions
explanation: Under Ind AS 37 Paragraph 72, a constructive obligation to restructure arises only when an entity: (a) has a detailed formal plan; and (b) has raised a valid expectation in those affected that it will carry out the restructuring by starting to implement that plan or announcing its main features to those affected. However, under Paragraph 81, a restructuring provision shall include only the direct expenditures arising from restructuring, and excludes costs associated with ongoing activities and future operating losses.

subject: Financial Reporting
topicTitle: Provisions, Contingent Liabilities, and Events After the Reporting Period
tag: [ICAI CA Final FR PYQ] Ind AS 37: Exclusion of Future Operating Losses
question: Due to the introduction of advanced competitive technology, management of Heritage Mills Ltd. projects that its traditional spinning division will incur operating losses of ₹15 Crores during FY 2024-25. Can management establish a provision for future operating losses of ₹15 Crores in the financial statements for FY 2023-24 under Ind AS 37?
options: Yes, prudence mandates recognizing anticipated future operating losses immediately.

No, Ind AS 37 Paragraph 63 explicitly states that provisions shall not be recognized for future operating losses, because they do not meet the definition of a liability (no past event creating a present obligation) and the general recognition criteria.
Yes, if approved by the Audit Committee.
Permissible if credited to General Reserve.
ref: Ind AS 37 - Paragraphs 63-65: Future Operating Losses
explanation: Ind AS 37 Paragraph 63 states unequivocally: 'Provisions shall not be recognized for future operating losses.' Future operating losses do not meet the definition of a liability under the Conceptual Framework or Ind AS 37 because there is no present obligation resulting from a past event. An expectation of future operating losses is an indicator that certain assets of the operation may be impaired under Ind AS 36.

subject: Financial Reporting
topicTitle: Provisions, Contingent Liabilities, and Events After the Reporting Period
tag: [ICAI CA Final FR PYQ] Ind AS 37: Onerous Contract - Incremental Cost vs Cost of Fulfilling
question: BuildFast Ltd. enters into a non-cancellable operating supply contract to supply 10,000 units of components at ₹100 each (total revenue ₹10,00,000). Due to raw material inflation, the direct incremental cost to manufacture the units is ₹12,00,000, and allocated factory overheads are ₹2,00,000 (total cost of fulfilling ₹14,00,000). The contractual penalty for terminating the contract without performance is ₹3,00,000. Under the revised Ind AS 37 amendments on onerous contracts, what is the provision for onerous contract to be recognized?
options: ₹4,00,000 (Cost of fulfilling ₹14,00,000 minus revenue ₹10,00,000).
₹3,00,000 (measured at the lower of the net cost of fulfilling the contract ₹4,00,000 and the penalty arising from failure to fulfill ₹3,00,000).
₹2,00,000 (incremental cost ₹12,00,000 minus revenue ₹10,00,000).
Zero provision because revenue is still positive.
ref: Ind AS 37 - Paragraphs 66-69: Onerous Contracts & Definition of Cost of Fulfilling
explanation: Ind AS 37 defines an onerous contract as a contract in which the unavoidable costs of meeting the obligations under the contract exceed the economic benefits expected to be received. The unavoidable costs under a contract reflect the least net cost of exiting from the contract, which is the lower of the cost of fulfilling it and any compensation or penalties arising from failure to fulfill it. Here, least net cost = Lower of (₹4,00,000 net fulfillment cost and ₹3,00,000 termination penalty) = ₹3,00,000.

subject: Financial Reporting
topicTitle: Provisions, Contingent Liabilities, and Events After the Reporting Period
tag: [ICAI CA Final FR PYQ] Ind AS 37: Reimbursements & Third-Party Claims
question: Chemicals India Ltd. faces a product liability claim of ₹10 Crores on 31st March 2024. Legal experts confirm it is probable (70% likelihood) that the entity will be held liable for ₹10 Crores. Chemicals India Ltd. holds a comprehensive insurance policy with New India Assurance, and the insurer has formally confirmed in writing that it will reimburse 80% of any court-awarded damages up to ₹8 Crores. How should the provision and reimbursement be presented under Ind AS 37?
options: Present a net provision of ₹2 Crores in the balance sheet, with no other disclosure.

Recognize a gross provision of ₹10 Crores under liabilities on the balance sheet, and recognize a separate reimbursement asset of ₹8 Crores under assets (virtually certain of receipt); in the statement of profit and loss, the expense may be presented net of the reimbursement (₹2 Crores net expense).
No provision is recognized because the insurance coverage covers the majority of the risk.
Recognize an asset of ₹10 Crores and liability of ₹8 Crores.
ref: Ind AS 37 - Paragraphs 53-54: Reimbursements by Third Parties
explanation: Under Ind AS 37 Paragraph 53, where some or all of the expenditure required to settle a provision is expected to be reimbursed by another party, the reimbursement shall be recognized when, and only when, it is virtually certain that reimbursement will be received if the entity settles the obligation. The reimbursement shall be treated as a separate asset on the balance sheet (not exceeding provision amount). In the statement of profit and loss, the expense relating to a provision may be presented net of the amount recognized for a reimbursement.

subject: Financial Reporting
topicTitle: Provisions, Contingent Liabilities, and Events After the Reporting Period
tag: [ICAI CA Final FR PYQ] Ind AS 37: Contingent Assets Recognition Threshold
question: Pharma Innovations Ltd. sued a competitor for patent infringement, claiming ₹50 Crores in damages. On 15th March 2024, the High Court ruled in Pharma Innovations' favour, awarding ₹40 Crores damages. On 25th March 2024, the competitor filed an appeal in the Supreme Court, and legal counsel advises that an inflow of economic benefits is 'probable' (65% likelihood) but not yet virtually certain until final disposal. How should Pharma Innovations Ltd. treat this matter on 31st March 2024 under Ind AS 37?
options: Recognize an asset and income of ₹40 Crores in Profit and Loss.
Do NOT recognize an asset in the balance sheet; disclose the contingent asset in the notes to financial statements, because the inflow of economic benefits is probable.
Recognize ₹40 Crores as Other Comprehensive Income.
Omit all disclosures until the Supreme Court final judgment.
ref: Ind AS 37 - Paragraphs 31-35: Contingent Assets
explanation: Ind AS 37 Paragraph 31 states: 'An entity shall not recognize a contingent asset.' Contingent assets are not recognized in financial statements since this may result in the recognition of income that may never be realized. However, when the inflow of economic benefits is probable, an entity discloses a brief description of the contingent asset in the notes. Only when the realization of income is virtually certain is the related asset no longer a contingent asset and its recognition appropriate.

subject: Financial Reporting
topicTitle: Provisions, Contingent Liabilities, and Events After the Reporting Period
tag: [ICAI CA Final FR PYQ] Ind AS 10: Adjusting Event - Insolvency of Customer Post Balance Sheet Date
question: On 31st March 2024, Delta Traders had a trade receivable of ₹15 Lakhs due from retail customer Horizon Ltd. Horizon Ltd. had been operating normally. On 20th April 2024 (prior to the approval of financial statements by the Board on 25th May 2024), Horizon Ltd. was declared insolvent by the NCLT due to financial deterioration that had been worsening over the past year. Is this an adjusting or non-adjusting event under Ind AS 10?
options: Non-adjusting event, because insolvency was formally declared after 31st March 2024.

Adjusting event, because the bankruptcy of a customer that occurs after the reporting period usually confirms that the customer was in financial distress and credit-impaired at the end of the reporting period; Delta Traders must adjust the carrying amount of the trade receivable on 31st March 2024 by recognizing an expected credit loss/bad debt provision.
Adjusting event only if Horizon Ltd. is a related party.
Disclosed as a contingent asset.
ref: Ind AS 10 (Events After the Reporting Period) - Paragraph 9(b)(i): Bankruptcy of Customer as Adjusting Event
explanation: Ind AS 10 Paragraph 9(b)(i) explicitly cites as an example of an adjusting event: 'The bankruptcy of a customer that occurs after the reporting period usually confirms that the customer was credit-impaired at the end of the reporting period, and that the entity needs to adjust the carrying amount of the trade receivable.' Financial statements for FY 2023-24 must be adjusted.

subject: Financial Reporting
topicTitle: Provisions, Contingent Liabilities, and Events After the Reporting Period
tag: [ICAI CA Final FR PYQ] Ind AS 10: Non-Adjusting Event - Fire / Destruction of Plant
question: On 10th April 2024 (after the reporting date of 31st March 2024, but before approval of financial statements by the Board on 20th May 2024), an accidental fire completely destroyed a major manufacturing warehouse of Zenith Ltd., causing an uninsured inventory loss of ₹20 Crores. The going concern of Zenith Ltd. is NOT impaired. How should this fire loss be reported in the financial statements for the year ended 31st March 2024?
options: Adjust the balance sheet as of 31st March 2024 by writing down inventory by ₹20 Crores.

It is a Non-Adjusting Event, because the fire occurred after the reporting period and does not relate to conditions that existed on 31st March 2024; no adjustment is made to the balance sheet, but details and estimated financial effect must be disclosed in the notes to financial statements.
Ignore completely in FY 2023-24 financial statements.
Recognize an exceptional expense in OCI for FY 2023-24.
ref: Ind AS 10 - Paragraph 10 & Paragraph 22(d): Non-Adjusting Events
explanation: Under Ind AS 10, non-adjusting events are those that are indicative of conditions that arose after the reporting period. Paragraph 22(d) explicitly provides 'the destruction of a major production plant by a fire after the reporting period' as an example of a non-adjusting event. If material, non-adjusting events do not alter balance sheet figures, but require disclosure of the nature of the event and an estimate of its financial effect.

subject: Financial Reporting
topicTitle: Provisions, Contingent Liabilities, and Events After the Reporting Period
tag: [ICAI CA Final FR PYQ] Ind AS 10: Dividends Declared After Reporting Period
question: On 15th May 2024, the Board of Directors of Infosys Ltd. proposed a final dividend of ₹15 per equity share (total payout ₹600 Crores) for the financial year ended 31st March 2024. The dividend is subject to approval by shareholders at the forthcoming Annual General Meeting (AGM) in July 2024. How should the proposed dividend be accounted for in the financial statements for the year ended 31st March 2024 under Ind AS 10 and Ind AS 1?
options: Recognized as a Current Liability on the balance sheet as of 31st March 2024.

Not recognized as a liability on the balance sheet as of 31st March 2024 because no obligation existed at the reporting date; disclosed in the notes to financial statements in accordance with Ind AS 1.
Deducted directly from Cash and Cash Equivalents on 31st March 2024.
Recognized in Other Comprehensive Income.
ref: Ind AS 10 - Paragraphs 12-13 & Ind AS 1 Paragraph 137: Dividends Declared After Reporting Period
explanation: Ind AS 10 Paragraph 12 states: 'If an entity declares dividends to holders of equity instruments after the reporting period, the entity shall not recognize those dividends as a liability at the end of the reporting period.' Because they do not meet the criteria of a present obligation on the balance sheet date, proposed dividends are disclosed in the notes.

subject: Financial Reporting
topicTitle: Provisions, Contingent Liabilities, and Events After the Reporting Period
tag: [ICAI CA Final FR PYQ] Ind AS 10: Deterioration in Operating Results and Going Concern
question: Between 31st March 2024 and 10th May 2024 (prior to the signing of the audit report), global commodity prices crashed by 80%, causing the sole operating refinery of Petroworks Ltd. to become unviable. The Board resolved to cease operations and liquidate the company in June 2024. How does this event affect the financial statements for the year ended 31st March 2024 under Ind AS 10?
options: It is a non-adjusting event because the market price collapse occurred in April/May 2024; disclose in notes only.

It overrides the normal non-adjusting classification: Ind AS 10 mandates that an entity shall NOT prepare its financial statements on a going concern basis if management determines after the reporting period that it intends to liquidate the entity or cease trading; financial statements for FY 2023-24 must be prepared on a non-going concern (liquidation/realizable value) basis.
