Investor Ltd. has no legal or constructive obligation to fund further losses. What is the loss recognized by Investor Ltd. under Ind AS 28?
options: Recognize full loss of ₹16 Crores and establish a provision of ₹2 Crores under liabilities.

Recognize loss of ₹14 Crores: reducing the equity investment of ₹10 Crores to Nil, and reducing the long-term loan of ₹4 Crores to Nil; the remaining unabsorbed loss of ₹2 Crores is discontinued and disclosed off-balance sheet.
Recognize loss strictly up to the equity investment of ₹10 Crores, leaving the loan untouched.
Zero loss recognized until Associate is liquidated.
ref: Ind AS 28 - Paragraph 38: Losses in Excess of Investment
explanation: Under Ind AS 28 Paragraph 38, if an entity's share of losses of an associate equals or exceeds its interest in the associate, the entity discontinues recognizing its share of further losses. The interest in an associate is the carrying amount of the investment under the equity method together with any long-term interests that, in substance, form part of the entity's net investment (such as long-term loans). Losses are recognized until the net investment is reduced to zero.

subject: Financial Reporting
tag: [ICAI CA Final FR PYQ] Ind AS 111: Joint Arrangement Classification - Joint Operation vs Joint Venture
question: PetroIndia Ltd. and GasCorp Ltd. establish an unincorporated consortium 'DeepSea Joint Venture' to explore an offshore gas block. The legal contract specifies that the parties have joint control, each party has rights to the underlying pipeline and drilling assets in a 50:50 ratio, obligations for the liabilities incurred are borne directly 50:50, and gas output is shared in kind. How is this arrangement classified under Ind AS 111?
options: Joint Venture, accounted for using the equity method under Ind AS 28.

Joint Operation, because the parties have direct rights to the assets and direct obligations for the liabilities relating to the arrangement; each party recognizes its share of assets, liabilities, revenues, and expenses directly on its balance sheet.
Subsidiary of PetroIndia Ltd.
Financial Instrument under Ind AS 109.
ref: Ind AS 111 (Joint Arrangements) - Paragraphs 14-16 & Appendix B
explanation: Ind AS 111 classifies a joint arrangement as either a joint operation or a joint venture based on the rights and obligations of the parties. A joint operation is a joint arrangement whereby the parties that have joint control of the arrangement have rights to the assets, and obligations for the liabilities, relating to the arrangement. Parties recognize their share of assets, liabilities, revenues and expenses line-by-line.

subject: Financial Reporting
tag: [ICAI CA Final FR PYQ] Ind AS 111: Joint Venture Accounting Method
question: How does Ind AS 111 and Ind AS 28 mandate the accounting treatment for an investment in a 'Joint Venture' in an entity's consolidated financial statements?
options: Proportionate Consolidation (line-by-line consolidation of 50% assets and liabilities).
Equity Method in accordance with Ind AS 28 (single line-item on balance sheet and single line-item in P&L for share of profit/loss).
Fair Value Through Profit or Loss under Ind AS 109.
Cost Model under Ind AS 27.
ref: Ind AS 111 - Paragraph 24 & Ind AS 28: Equity Method for Joint Ventures
explanation: Ind AS 111 Paragraph 24 states: 'A joint venturer shall recognize its interest in a joint venture as an investment and shall account for that investment using the equity method in accordance with Ind AS 28.' Proportionate consolidation is prohibited under Ind AS.

subject: Financial Reporting
tag: [ICAI CA Final FR PYQ] Ind AS 28: Discontinuation of Equity Method
question: Parent Ltd. owns 35% of Associate Ltd. On 1st October 2023, Parent Ltd. sells 25% of Associate Ltd. for ₹50 Crores, retaining a 10% equity holding (fair value ₹20 Crores). Carrying amount of the 35% holding prior to sale was ₹42 Crores. With the 10% holding, Parent Ltd. loses significant influence. How should the transaction be accounted for under Ind AS 28?
options: The retained 10% is carried forward at historical cost of ₹12 Crores.

An entity shall discontinue the use of the equity method from the date when its investment ceases to be an associate; it measures the retained 10% interest at fair value (₹20 Cr); the total gain recognized in Profit or Loss is ₹28 Crores (Consideration ₹50 Cr + Retained fair value ₹20 Cr - Carrying amount ₹42 Cr).
All proceeds are credited to Capital Reserve.
No gain or loss is recognized until the remaining 10% is sold.
ref: Ind AS 28 - Paragraph 22: Discontinuance of the Equity Method
explanation: Under Ind AS 28 Paragraph 22, an entity shall discontinue the use of the equity method from the date when its investment ceases to be an associate. On the loss of significant influence, the investor shall measure at fair value any investment the investor retains in the former associate. The investor recognizes in profit or loss the difference between: (a) the fair value of any retained interest plus proceeds from disposal; and (b) the carrying amount of the investment at the date the equity method was discontinued.

subject: Financial Reporting
tag: [ICAI CA Final FR PYQ] Ind AS 111: Operator of a Joint Operation Accounting
question: Alpha Ltd. is the operator of a 50:50 Joint Operation with Beta Ltd. Alpha Ltd. purchases materials of ₹10 Crores on behalf of the joint operation and bills Beta Ltd. for its ₹5 Crores share. Alpha Ltd. does not charge a management fee or margin. How does Alpha Ltd. present this transaction in its statement of profit and loss?
options: Alpha Ltd. records ₹10 Crores as revenue and ₹10 Crores as cost of sales.

Alpha Ltd. recognizes only its own 50% share of costs (₹5 Crores) as an expense; the ₹5 Crores reimbursement from Beta Ltd. is not treated as revenue, because Alpha Ltd. acts as an agent in billing the co-venturer.
Alpha Ltd. records ₹5 Crores as other operating revenue.
Alpha Ltd. recognizes the full ₹10 Crores as inventory.
ref: Ind AS 111 - Paragraphs 20-22 & B34-B37: Accounting for Joint Operations
explanation: Under Ind AS 111, a joint operator accounts for its own share of assets, liabilities, revenues, and expenses. When an operator acts on behalf of the joint operation and receives reimbursements for costs incurred without margin, the operator acts as an agent; it does not report gross revenues and costs, but reflects only its net contractual share of expenses.

subject: Financial Reporting
tag: [ICAI CA Final FR PYQ] Ind AS 28: Impairment of Investment in Associate
question: Investor Ltd. holds an associate with a carrying amount of ₹100 Crores (which includes implicit goodwill of ₹25 Crores determined at initial acquisition). The associate suffers an economic downturn. How is the investment tested for impairment under Ind AS 28 and Ind AS 36?
options: Goodwill of ₹25 Crores must be tested separately for impairment every year.

Because implicit goodwill forms part of the carrying amount of the net investment in the associate, it is NOT tested separately for impairment; instead, the entire carrying amount of the investment is tested for impairment as a single asset under Ind AS 36 by comparing its recoverable amount (higher of value in use and fair value less costs of disposal) with its carrying amount.
Associates are exempt from impairment testing under Ind AS.
Impairment is allocated strictly to implicit goodwill first.
ref: Ind AS 28 - Paragraphs 40-42: Impairment Testing of Associates
explanation: Ind AS 28 Paragraph 42 states: 'Because goodwill that forms part of the carrying amount of an investment in an associate or a joint venture is not separately recognized, it is not tested for impairment separately by applying the requirements for impairment testing goodwill in Ind AS 36. Instead, the entire carrying amount of the investment is tested for impairment in accordance with Ind AS 36 as a single asset.'

subject: Financial Reporting
tag: [ICAI CA Final FR PYQ] Ind AS 28: Differences in Reporting Dates
question: The financial statements of an associate are prepared to 31st December each year, whereas the investor's reporting date is 31st March. Under Ind AS 28, what are the requirements regarding the time lag and adjustments?
options: The associate must change its statutory financial year to 31st March immediately.

The difference between the reporting date of the associate and that of the investor shall be no more than three months; adjustments must be made for the effects of significant transactions or events that occur between that date and the date of the investor's financial statements.
A time lag of up to 12 months is permissible without adjustments.
The investor must consolidate the associate using budgeted numbers.
ref: Ind AS 28 - Paragraphs 33-34: Difference in Reporting Dates
explanation: Under Ind AS 28 Paragraph 34, when the financial statements of an associate or joint venture used in applying the equity method are prepared as of a date different from that used by the entity, the difference between the end of the reporting period of the associate and that of the entity shall be no more than three months. The length of reporting periods and any difference between the ends of the reporting periods shall be the same from period to period.

subject: Financial Reporting
tag: [ICAI CA Final FR PYQ] Ind AS 111: Separate Legal Vehicle Assessment
question: When a joint arrangement is structured through a separate legal entity (e.g. a private limited company incorporated under the Companies Act 2013), what is the primary consideration in determining whether it is a Joint Venture or a Joint Operation?
options: The presence of a separate legal vehicle automatically makes it a Joint Operation.

The separate vehicle provides a legal separation between the vehicle and its owners, causing the assets and liabilities to be those of the separate vehicle; it is classified as a Joint Venture unless the legal form, contractual terms, or other facts and circumstances give the parties direct rights to the assets and obligations for the liabilities.
All incorporated entities are treated as subsidiaries under Ind AS 110.
Classification depends solely on the capital contribution percentage.
ref: Ind AS 111 - Paragraph B16-B33: Assessing Joint Arrangement Structure
explanation: When a joint arrangement is structured through a separate vehicle, the legal form initially confers rights to net assets (Joint Venture). However, the parties must assess whether contractual terms or other facts and circumstances (e.g. parties taking all output and financing debt) override the legal form to give direct rights to assets and obligations for liabilities (Joint Operation).

subject: Financial Reporting
tag: [ICAI CA Final FR PYQ] Ind AS 28: Inter-Company Dividends from Associate
question: Associate Ltd. declares and pays a cash dividend of ₹10 Crores to its shareholders. Investor Ltd. holds a 30% equity stake (receiving ₹3 Crores). How should Investor Ltd. record this ₹3 Crores cash dividend under the equity method in its consolidated financial statements?
options: Recognize ₹3 Crores as Dividend Income in the Statement of Profit and Loss.

Debit Cash ₹3 Crores and Credit Investment in Associate ₹3 Crores (reducing the carrying amount of the investment, because distributions received from an investee reduce the carrying amount of the investment under the equity method).
Credit Other Comprehensive Income ₹3 Crores.
Credit Retained Earnings directly.
ref: Ind AS 28 - Paragraph 10: Distributions Under the Equity Method
explanation: Under the equity method defined in Ind AS 28 Paragraph 10, the investment in an associate or a joint venture is initially recognized at cost and adjusted thereafter for the post-acquisition change in the investor's share of the investee's net assets. Distributions (dividends) received from an investee reduce the carrying amount of the investment.

subject: Financial Reporting
tag: [ICAI CA Final FR PYQ] Ind AS 28: Potential Voting Rights in Assessing Significant Influence
question: Investor Ltd. holds 15% voting equity shares in Target Ltd., but also holds currently exercisable share warrants that, if exercised, would immediately increase its holding to 25%. How do these potential voting rights affect significant influence under Ind AS 28?
options: Potential voting rights are not considered under Ind AS 28.

Currently exercisable potential voting rights that are substantive are considered when assessing whether an entity has significant influence; because the warrants are currently exercisable and substantive, they demonstrate that Investor Ltd. has significant influence.
Investor Ltd. must recognize control.
Warrants must be exercised before significant influence can be claimed.
ref: Ind AS 28 - Paragraphs 7-8: Potential Voting Rights
explanation: Ind AS 28 Paragraph 7 states: 'An entity may own share warrants, share call options, debt or equity instruments that are convertible into ordinary shares... The existence and effect of potential voting rights that are currently exercisable or convertible, including potential voting rights held by other entities, are considered when assessing whether an entity has significant influence.'

subject: Financial Reporting
tag: [ICAI CA Final FR PYQ] Ind AS 111: Accounting for Sales/Contributions of Assets to Joint Operation
question: A joint operator enters into a transaction with a joint operation to sell an item of machinery (cost ₹40 Lakhs) for ₹60 Lakhs (gain ₹20 Lakhs). The joint operator holds a 40% interest in the joint operation. At year-end, the machinery is still held by the joint operation. What gain on sale does the joint operator recognize in its profit or loss?
options: Full gain of ₹20 Lakhs.

₹12 Lakhs (the operator recognizes gains and losses resulting from such a transaction only to the extent of the other parties' interests in the joint operation: 60% of ₹20 Lakhs = ₹12 Lakhs; its own 40% share of ₹8 Lakhs is eliminated).
Zero gain until the machinery is sold to an independent third party.
₹8 Lakhs.
ref: Ind AS 111 - Paragraph B34: Sales of Assets to a Joint Operation
explanation: Under Ind AS 111 Paragraph B34, when an entity enters into a transaction with a joint operation in which it is a joint operator, such as a sale or contribution of assets, it is conducting the transaction with the other parties to the joint operation. The joint operator shall recognize gains and losses resulting from such a transaction only to the extent of the other parties' interests in the joint operation.

subject: Financial Reporting
tag: [ICAI CA Final FR PYQ] Ind AS 28: Other Comprehensive Income of an Associate
question: During the year, Associate Ltd. recognizes a revaluation gain on land of ₹10 Crores in Other Comprehensive Income (OCI). Investor Ltd. holds a 25% stake in Associate Ltd. How does Investor Ltd. record its 25% share (₹2.5 Crores) in its consolidated financial statements?
options: Recognized as operating revenue in Profit or Loss.
Recognized in Other Comprehensive Income (OCI) as Investor's share of OCI of associate, and added to the carrying amount of the Investment in Associate.
Deferred as a liability on the balance sheet.
Deducted from goodwill.
ref: Ind AS 28 - Paragraph 10: Share of OCI of an Associate
explanation: Ind AS 28 Paragraph 10 states: 'The investor's share of the investee's profit or loss is recognized in the investor's profit or loss. The investor's share of the investee's other comprehensive income is recognized in the investor's other comprehensive income.' The entry debits Investment in Associate and credits Share of OCI of Associate.

subject: Financial Reporting
tag: [ICAI CA Final FR PYQ] Ind AS 111: Reclassification from Joint Venture to Joint Operation
question: If contractual terms of a joint arrangement are amended such that the parties now have direct rights to the assets and direct obligations for the liabilities of the arrangement, how is the transition from Joint Venture to Joint Operation accounted for?
options: The entity continues using the equity method under grandfathering rules.
The entity derecognizes the investment in the joint venture and recognizes its share of each asset and liability of the joint operation, recognizing any difference in Profit or Loss.
The entity consolidates the arrangement as a subsidiary.
Accounted for as a prior period error.
ref: Ind AS 111 - Transition and Reclassification Rules
explanation: When an arrangement changes from a joint venture to a joint operation, the entity ceases applying the equity method and begins recognizing its proportionate share of assets, liabilities, revenues, and expenses. Any difference between the net carrying amount of the derecognized investment and the net identifiable assets recognized is recognized in profit or loss.

subject: Financial Reporting
tag: [ICAI CA Final FR PYQ] Ind AS 28: Investment in Associate Held for Sale (Ind AS 105)
question: On 1st January 2024, the Board of Directors of Investor Ltd. committed to a plan to sell its entire 30% investment in Associate Ltd. within 6 months. The criteria for classification as 'Held for Sale' under Ind AS 105 are met. How should the investment in the associate be accounted for from 1st January 2024?
options: Continue applying the equity method until the sale is completed.

Discontinue the equity method; measure the investment at the lower of its carrying amount under equity method at classification date and fair value less costs to sell, and present it separately as a Non-Current Asset Held for Sale under current assets.
Write off the investment immediately to Profit or Loss.
Transfer the investment to FVTPL.
ref: Ind AS 28 - Paragraph 20 & Ind AS 105: Associates Held for Sale
explanation: Under Ind AS 28 Paragraph 20, an entity shall apply Ind AS 105 to an investment, or a portion of an investment, in an associate or a joint venture that meets the criteria to be classified as held for sale. The equity method ceases on the date of classification as held for sale, and the asset is measured under Ind AS 105 at the lower of carrying amount and fair value less costs to sell.

subject: Financial Reporting
tag: [ICAI CA Final FR PYQ] Ind AS 111: Joint Operator Acquiring an Interest in a Joint Operation Constituting a Business
question: Alpha Ltd. acquires a 30% interest in a Joint Operation whose activity constitutes a business as defined in Ind AS 103. How must Alpha Ltd. account for the acquisition of this interest under Ind AS 111?
options: Account for it strictly at historical cash paid without purchase price allocation.

Apply all of the principles on business combinations accounting in Ind AS 103 (recognizing identifiable assets and liabilities at fair value, measuring transaction costs as expenses, and recognizing goodwill or bargain purchase gain).
Account for it as an associate under Ind AS 28.
Exclude it from financial statements.
ref: Ind AS 111 - Paragraph 21A & Paragraph B33A: Joint Operation Constituting a Business
explanation: Ind AS 111 Paragraph 21A states: 'When an entity acquires an interest in a joint operation in which the activity of the joint operation constitutes a business, as defined in Ind AS 103, it shall apply, to the extent of its share, all of the principles on business combinations accounting in Ind AS 103, and other Ind ASs that do not conflict with the guidance in this Ind AS.' Goodwill is recognized on the acquisition.

subject: Financial Reporting
tag: [ICAI CA Final FR PYQ] Ind AS 28: Presentation in Separate Financial Statements
question: In its Separate Financial Statements (prepared under Ind AS 27), how may an entity account for its investments in associates and joint ventures?
options: Exclusively using proportionate consolidation.
Either: (a) at cost; (b) in accordance with Ind AS 109 (at FVTPL or FVOCI); or (c) using the equity method as described in Ind AS 28.
Only at net realizable value.
Separate financial statements cannot include investments in associates.
ref: Ind AS 27 (Separate Financial Statements) - Paragraph 10
explanation: Under Ind AS 27 Paragraph 10, when an entity prepares separate financial statements, it shall account for investments in subsidiaries, joint ventures and associates either: (a) at cost; (b) in accordance with Ind AS 109; or (c) using the equity method as described in Ind AS 28. The entity shall apply the same accounting for each category of investments.

subject: Financial Reporting
tag: [ICAI CA Final FR PYQ] Ind AS 28: Goodwill Included in Investment in Associate
question: Investor Ltd. acquires a 25% stake in Target Ltd. for ₹50 Crores. The fair value of Target Ltd.'s identifiable net assets is ₹160 Crores (Investor's 25% share = ₹40 Crores). The excess ₹10 Crores represents implicit goodwill. How is this ₹10 Crores presented on Investor Ltd.'s balance sheet?
options: Presented separately as a distinct Goodwill line item under Intangible Assets.
Included in the carrying amount of the investment in the associate (total investment presented as ₹50 Crores); separate presentation of goodwill and amortization of goodwill are both prohibited.
Expensed immediately in Profit or Loss.
Deducted from Other Equity.
ref: Ind AS 28 - Paragraph 32(a): Implicit Goodwill in Associate
explanation: Ind AS 28 Paragraph 32(a) states: 'Goodwill relating to an associate or a joint venture is included in the carrying amount of the investment. Amortization of that goodwill is not permitted.' Goodwill is not recognized as a separate asset on the balance sheet, but remains embedded within the single line-item 'Investment in Associates'.

subject: Financial Reporting
tag: [ICAI CA Final FR PYQ] Ind AS 21: Determination of Functional Currency - Primary vs Secondary Factors
question: Global Exports Ltd. is incorporated in India. 85% of its sales revenues are invoiced and collected in US Dollars (USD). Labor, materials, and local compliance costs are incurred and settled in Indian Rupees (INR). Financing was raised in USD bonds on the Singapore exchange. Under Ind AS 21, what are the primary factors in determining the functional currency?
options: The currency of the country in which the registered corporate office is situated (INR).

The currency that mainly influences sales prices for goods and services, and the currency of the country whose competitive forces and regulations mainly determine the sales prices, along with the currency that mainly influences labor, material, and other operating costs.
The currency chosen by the Board of Directors.
The presentation currency of the parent company.
ref: Ind AS 21 (The Effects of Changes in Foreign Exchange Rates) - Paragraphs 9-10: Primary Factors for Functional Currency
explanation: Ind AS 21 Paragraph 9 states that the primary factors are: (a) the currency that mainly influences sales prices for goods and services; and (b) the currency of the country whose competitive forces and regulations determine sales prices; and (c) the currency that mainly influences labor, material and other costs of providing goods or services. Secondary factors include financing and operating cash flow retention.

subject: Financial Reporting
tag: [ICAI CA Final FR PYQ] Ind AS 21: Monetary vs Non-Monetary Items at Reporting Date
question: On 31st March 2024, an Indian entity (functional currency INR) holds the following foreign currency items denominated in USD: (i) Trade Receivables of $100,000; (ii) Foreign equity investment at FVOCI of $50,000; (iii) Inventory acquired for $40,000 carried at cost; and (iv) Trade Payables of $80,000. Which of these are 'monetary items' to be translated at the closing spot exchange rate under Ind AS 21?
options: All four items.

Trade Receivables ($100,000) and Trade Payables ($80,000) are monetary items translated at the closing rate with exchange differences to P&L; Inventory (cost) and Equity at FVOCI are non-monetary items.
Only the equity investment.
Only Trade Receivables.
ref: Ind AS 21 - Paragraphs 16 & 23: Monetary vs Non-Monetary Items
explanation: Ind AS 21 defines monetary items as units of currency held and assets and liabilities to be received or paid in a fixed or determinable number of units of currency (e.g. receivables, cash, payables). Non-monetary items have the absence of a right to receive or deliver a fixed number of units of currency (inventory, PPE, equity investments). Monetary items are translated at the closing rate with exchange differences recognized in profit or loss.

subject: Financial Reporting
tag: [ICAI CA Final FR PYQ] Ind AS 21: Non-Monetary Item Carried at Fair Value
question: An entity holds an investment property in London denominated in British Pounds (GBP). It measures the property at Fair Value under Ind AS 40 / Ind AS 113. On 31st March 2024, the fair value is determined in GBP. At what exchange rate should the property be translated into INR, and where is the resulting foreign exchange difference recognized?
options: Historical exchange rate at the date of original acquisition; gain to P&L.

Exchange rate at the date when the fair value was determined (closing rate); the exchange difference is recognized in the Statement of Profit and Loss (in the same manner as the fair value gain or loss under Ind AS 40).
Average exchange rate for the year; difference to OCI.
Historical cost rate without any translation.
ref: Ind AS 21 - Paragraphs 23(c) & 30: Non-Monetary Items Measured at Fair Value
explanation: Ind AS 21 Paragraph 23(c) states that non-monetary items that are measured at fair value in a foreign currency shall be translated using the exchange rates at the date when the fair value was measured. Under Paragraph 30, when a gain or loss on a non-monetary item is recognized in profit or loss, any exchange component of that gain or loss shall be recognized in profit or loss.

subject: Financial Reporting
tag: [ICAI CA Final FR PYQ] Ind AS 21: Translation of Foreign Operation to Presentation Currency
question: Indian Parent Ltd. (INR presentation currency) consolidates its 100% US subsidiary (USD functional currency). In translating the US subsidiary's balance sheet and P&L into INR under Ind AS 21, what exchange rates must be applied?
options: All assets, liabilities, income, and expenses are translated at the closing exchange rate.

Assets and liabilities (both monetary and non-monetary) are translated at the closing rate at the date of that balance sheet; income and expenses are translated at exchange rates at the dates of the transactions (or an appropriate average rate); all resulting exchange differences are recognized in Other Comprehensive Income (Foreign Currency Translation Reserve - FCTR).
All items translated at historical rates.
Assets at historical rate, liabilities at closing rate.
ref: Ind AS 21 - Paragraphs 39-40: Translation to Presentation Currency
explanation: Under Ind AS 21 Paragraph 39: (a) assets and liabilities for each balance sheet presented shall be translated at the closing rate at the date of that balance sheet; (b) income and expenses for each statement of profit and loss shall be translated at exchange rates at the dates of the transactions (average rate); and (c) all resulting exchange differences shall be recognized in Other Comprehensive Income (accumulated in FCTR).

subject: Financial Reporting
tag: [ICAI CA Final FR PYQ] Ind AS 21: Recycling of Foreign Currency Translation Reserve (FCTR)
question: Indian Parent Ltd. sells its entire 100% equity stake in its US subsidiary. Over the 5-year holding period, cumulative foreign currency translation gains of ₹50 Crores had been recognized in OCI and accumulated in FCTR. How is the accumulated FCTR treated upon full disposal of the foreign operation under Ind AS 21?
options: Retained permanently in equity without reclassification.

Reclassified ('recycled') in full from Other Comprehensive Income (FCTR) to the Statement of Profit and Loss as a reclassification adjustment within the total gain or loss on disposal of the foreign operation.
Transferred directly to Securities Premium.
Written off against goodwill.
ref: Ind AS 21 - Paragraph 48: Disposal of a Foreign Operation and Recycling of FCTR
explanation: Ind AS 21 Paragraph 48 states: 'On the disposal of a foreign operation, the cumulative amount of the exchange differences relating to that foreign operation, recognized in other comprehensive income and accumulated in the separate component of equity, shall be reclassified from equity to profit or loss (as a reclassification adjustment) when the gain or loss on disposal is recognized.'

subject: Financial Reporting
tag: [ICAI CA Final FR PYQ] Ind AS 21: Net Investment in a Foreign Operation
question: Indian Parent Ltd. extends an interest-free loan of $10,000,000 to its wholly-owned UK subsidiary. The loan agreement specifies that repayment is neither planned nor likely to occur in the foreseeable future. In substance, the loan forms part of Parent Ltd.'s net investment in the UK subsidiary. In the consolidated financial statements of the group, where are the foreign exchange differences on this loan recognized under Ind AS 21?
options: Recognized in the Consolidated Statement of Profit and Loss.
Recognized in Other Comprehensive Income (OCI) and accumulated in the Foreign Currency Translation Reserve (FCTR), to be reclassified to profit or loss on disposal of the net investment.
Recognized as an addition to share capital.
Eliminated against inter-company revenue.
ref: Ind AS 21 - Paragraphs 15 & 32: Monetary Item Forming Part of Net Investment
explanation: Ind AS 21 Paragraph 15 defines an item for which settlement is neither planned nor likely to occur in the foreseeable future as, in substance, part of the entity's net investment in that foreign operation. Under Paragraph 32, exchange differences arising on such monetary items in consolidated financial statements shall be recognized initially in Other Comprehensive Income and reclassified to profit or loss on disposal.

subject: Financial Reporting
tag: [ICAI CA Final FR PYQ] Ind AS 29: Indicators of Hyperinflation
question: Which of the following economic conditions is a key characteristic of a hyperinflationary economy under Ind AS 29?
options: Annual GDP growth exceeds 10%.

The cumulative inflation rate over a three-year period is approaching, or exceeds, 100%, and the general population prefers to keep its wealth in non-monetary assets or in a relatively stable foreign currency.
The central bank increases interest rates by 25 basis points.
Stock market valuations decline for two consecutive quarters.
ref: Ind AS 29 (Financial Reporting in Hyperinflationary Economies) - Paragraph 3: Indicators of Hyperinflation
explanation: Ind AS 29 Paragraph 3 lists characteristics of hyperinflation: (a) general population prefers wealth in non-monetary assets or stable foreign currency; (b) prices quoted in foreign currency; (c) credit sales compensate for expected loss of purchasing power; (d) interest rates and wages linked to a price index; and (e) the cumulative inflation rate over three years is approaching, or exceeds, 100%.

subject: Financial Reporting
tag: [ICAI CA Final FR PYQ] Ind AS 29: Restatement of Financial Statements
question: Under Ind AS 29, when an entity's functional currency is the currency of a hyperinflationary economy, how are its financial statements stated?
options: Stated in terms of the measuring unit current at the end of the reporting period by applying a General Price Index to non-monetary items, with the gain or loss on the net monetary position recognized in Profit or Loss.
Translated into USD at the historical exchange rate of 10 years ago.
Prepared strictly on a cash basis.
Non-monetary items are frozen at book value.
ref: Ind AS 29 - Paragraphs 8-9: Restatement in Constant Currency
explanation: Under Ind AS 29, the financial statements of an entity whose functional currency is hyperinflationary are stated in terms of the measuring unit current at the end of the reporting period. Balance sheet non-monetary items not already expressed in current measuring units are restated using a general price index. The gain or loss on the net monetary position is recognized in profit or loss.

subject: Financial Reporting
tag: [ICAI CA Final FR PYQ] Ind AS 21: Advance Payments for Non-Monetary Assets (Appendix B / IFRIC 22)
question: On 1st February 2024, Indian Importer Ltd. pays a non-refundable advance of $100,000 (exchange rate $1 = ₹82) to a US machine vendor for customized equipment. On 31st March 2024, the exchange rate is $1 = ₹84. On 15th April 2024 (when $1 = ₹85), the machinery is delivered. Under Appendix B of Ind AS 21, what is the initial cost of the machinery capitalized on 15th April 2024?
options: ₹82,00,000 ($100,000 × advance payment transaction date rate ₹82), because the date of the transaction for the purpose of determining the exchange rate on initial recognition of the non-monetary asset is the date on which the entity initially recognized the non-monetary advance asset.
Average rate of ₹83.50.
ref: Ind AS 21 - Appendix B (Foreign Currency Transactions and Advance Consideration)
explanation: Appendix B Paragraph 8 states that the date of the transaction for the purpose of determining the exchange rate to use on initial recognition of the related asset, expense, or income is the date on which an entity initially recognizes the non-monetary asset or non-monetary liability arising from the payment or receipt of advance consideration. Because the advance was paid on 1st February at ₹82, that historical rate applies to the machinery.

subject: Financial Reporting
tag: [ICAI CA Final FR PYQ] Ind AS 21: Exchange Differences on Borrowing Costs
question: An entity borrows USD 10,000,000 on 1st April 2023 at 5% interest per annum to construct a qualifying manufacturing plant. Local INR borrowings would have carried interest at 10% per annum. During the year, the exchange rate moved from $1 = ₹80 to $1 = ₹83 (exchange loss ₹3 Crores). How much of the ₹3 Crores exchange loss can be capitalized under Ind AS 23 and Ind AS 21 as an adjustment to borrowing costs?
options: The entire ₹3 Crores exchange loss is capitalized.

The exchange difference is capitalized only to the extent that it represents an adjustment to interest costs (the difference between local borrowing costs of 10% on ₹80 Cr = ₹8 Cr, and foreign borrowing costs of 5% on ₹80 Cr = ₹4 Cr, meaning up to ₹4 Crores of exchange difference can be treated as borrowing cost); here, the full ₹3 Crores exchange loss is capitalized as borrowing cost.
Zero; all exchange differences are expensed to P&L under Ind AS 21.
Recognized in OCI.
ref: Ind AS 23 - Paragraph 6(e) & Ind AS 21: Exchange Differences as Borrowing Costs
explanation: Ind AS 23 Paragraph 6(e) states that borrowing costs include exchange differences arising from foreign currency borrowings to the extent that they are regarded as an adjustment to interest costs. The equivalent local borrowing cost is ₹80 Cr × 10% = ₹8 Cr. Foreign interest paid = $500,000 × ₹83 (approx ₹4.15 Cr). Since foreign interest + ₹3 Cr exchange loss = ₹7.15 Cr < ₹8 Cr, the entire ₹3 Cr exchange loss is treated as an adjustment to borrowing costs.

subject: Financial Reporting
tag: [ICAI CA Final FR PYQ] Ind AS 21: Change in Functional Currency
question: Due to a fundamental shift in business model, Star India Ltd.'s functional currency changed from INR to USD on 1st October 2023. Under Ind AS 21, how is a change in functional currency accounted for?
options: Retrospectively, restating all prior years as if USD had always been the functional currency.

Prospectively from the date of the change: the entity translates all items into the new functional currency using the exchange rate at the date of the change; the resulting translated amounts for non-monetary items are treated as their historical cost.
The change is prohibited under Indian Company Law.
Recognized directly in Retained Earnings.
ref: Ind AS 21 - Paragraphs 35-37: Accounting for a Change in Functional Currency
explanation: Ind AS 21 Paragraph 35 states that when there is a change in an entity's functional currency, the entity shall apply the translation procedures applicable to the new functional currency prospectively from the date of the change. All items are translated into the new functional currency at the spot rate on the date of change, and non-monetary items are treated as their new historical cost.

subject: Financial Reporting
tag: [ICAI CA Final FR PYQ] Ind AS 21: Foreign Currency Dividend Received from Subsidiary
question: Indian Parent receives a cash dividend of USD 1,000,000 from its US subsidiary. At the date of dividend receipt, the exchange rate is $1 = ₹83. In Parent Ltd.'s standalone financial statements, at what amount is dividend income recognized?
options: ₹8,30,00,000 (USD 1,000,000 translated at the spot exchange rate on the date of receipt/entitlement).
Historical exchange rate at which the initial share capital was invested.
Average exchange rate of the financial year.
Zero, because intra-group dividends are eliminated in standalone accounts.
ref: Ind AS 21 - Paragraph 21: Initial Recognition of Foreign Currency Transactions
explanation: A foreign currency transaction shall be recorded, on initial recognition in the functional currency, by applying to the foreign currency amount the spot exchange rate between the functional currency and the foreign currency at the date of the transaction. The dividend is recognized at $1M × ₹83 = ₹8.3 Crores.

subject: Financial Reporting
tag: [ICAI CA Final FR PYQ] Ind AS 21: Goodwill of a Foreign Operation
question: Indian Parent Ltd. acquired a French subsidiary whose functional currency is the Euro (EUR). In the purchase price allocation, goodwill of €10,000,000 arose on acquisition. Under Ind AS 21, how is this goodwill treated at each subsequent balance sheet date?
options: Treated as an asset of the Indian Parent and fixed permanently at the historical acquisition INR rate.

Treated as an asset of the foreign operation (Euro-denominated asset); it is expressed in the functional currency of the foreign operation and translated at the closing exchange rate at each reporting date, with exchange differences recognized in OCI (FCTR).
Amortized over 5 years.
Expensed in full in P&L.
ref: Ind AS 21 - Paragraph 47: Goodwill Arising on Acquisition of a Foreign Operation
explanation: Ind AS 21 Paragraph 47 states explicitly: 'Any goodwill arising on the acquisition of a foreign operation and any fair value adjustments to the carrying amounts of assets and liabilities arising on the acquisition of that foreign operation shall be treated as assets and liabilities of the foreign operation. Thus, they shall be expressed in the functional currency of the foreign operation and shall be translated at the closing rate.'

subject: Financial Reporting
tag: [ICAI CA Final FR PYQ] Ind AS 21: Long-Term Foreign Currency Monetary Item Exemption (FCMITDA)
question: Under Companies (Ind AS) Rules, Paragraph 46A of Ind AS 21 provides a transitional relief for long-term foreign currency monetary items recognized before 1st April 2016. Which option did it grant?
options: Mandatory hedging of all foreign debt.

The option to accumulate exchange differences relating to long-term foreign currency monetary items in a 'Foreign Currency Monetary Item Translation Difference Account' (FCMITDA) and amortize it over the life of the monetary item, or add/deduct it from the cost of depreciable capital assets.
Complete exemption from financial reporting.
Option to revalue monetary assets.
ref: Ind AS 21 - Paragraph 46A: Transitional Relief on Long-Term Foreign Currency Monetary Items
explanation: Paragraph 46A was inserted into Ind AS 21 in India to provide continuity for companies that had elected the option under AS 11 (Paragraph 46/46A). It permitted capitalizing foreign exchange differences on long-term foreign currency borrowings into the cost of depreciable assets or accumulating them in FCMITDA.

subject: Financial Reporting
tag: [ICAI CA Final FR PYQ] Ind AS 29: Monetary Loss Calculation
question: At the start of the year, an enterprise in a hyperinflationary economy holds cash and trade receivables of 1,00,000 local currency units (LCU) and bank debt of 40,000 LCU (net monetary asset = 60,000 LCU). The general price index doubles (100% inflation) during the year. What is the impact on the net monetary position?
options: A purchasing power gain of 60,000 LCU.
A net purchasing power loss on monetary assets of 60,000 LCU recognized in the Statement of Profit and Loss, because holding monetary assets during inflation results in a loss of purchasing power.
No gain or loss arises on monetary items.
Recognized in OCI.
ref: Ind AS 29 - Paragraph 9 & Paragraph 28: Gain or Loss on Net Monetary Position
explanation: In a period of inflation, an entity holding an excess of monetary assets over monetary liabilities loses purchasing power, and an entity with an excess of monetary liabilities over monetary assets gains purchasing power to the extent the obligations are not linked to a price level. The resulting gain or loss on the net monetary position is recognized in profit or loss.

subject: Financial Reporting
tag: [ICAI CA Final FR PYQ] Ind AS 21: Foreign Currency Borrowings Fair Value Adjustment
question: An entity issues bonds denominated in Euro. The bond carries a fixed interest rate. When translating the foreign currency bond at the balance sheet date under Ind AS 21 (carried at amortized cost), how are the changes in exchange rate recognized?
options: In Other Comprehensive Income.
In the Statement of Profit and Loss as foreign exchange fluctuation gain or loss.
Deferred as a discount on bonds.
Adjusted against equity share capital.
ref: Ind AS 21 - Paragraph 28: Recognition of Exchange Differences on Monetary Items
explanation: Ind AS 21 Paragraph 28 specifies that exchange differences arising on the settlement of monetary items or on translating monetary items at rates different from those at which they were translated on initial recognition or in previous financial statements shall be recognized in profit or loss in the period in which they arise.

subject: Financial Reporting
tag: [ICAI CA Final FR PYQ] Ind AS 21: Presentation Currency Choice
question: An Indian corporate entity has INR as its functional currency. The Board of Directors wishes to present its consolidated financial statements in US Dollars (USD) to attract international institutional investors. Is this permissible under Ind AS 21?
options: No, Indian entities must always present their financial statements in Indian Rupees by law.

Yes, Ind AS 21 Paragraph 38 states that an entity may present its financial statements in any currency (or currencies); if the presentation currency differs from the functional currency, the entity translates its results and financial position into the presentation currency using standard translation procedures.
Permissible only if approved by the Reserve Bank of India.
Permissible only if turnover exceeds ₹10,000 Crores.
ref: Ind AS 21 - Paragraph 38: Choice of Presentation Currency
explanation: Ind AS 21 Paragraph 38 explicitly states: 'An entity may present its financial statements in any currency (or currencies).' If the presentation currency differs from the entity's functional currency, its results and financial position are translated into the presentation currency in accordance with paragraphs 39-43.

subject: Financial Reporting
tag: [ICAI CA Final FR PYQ] Ind AS 21: Partial Disposal of Subsidiary with FCTR Allocation
question: Parent Ltd. sells a 20% stake in its wholly-owned foreign subsidiary for ₹30 Crores, reducing its ownership from 100% to 80% without losing control. Cumulative FCTR relating to the subsidiary is ₹10 Crores. How is FCTR treated on this partial disposal?
options: ₹2 Crores (20% of FCTR) is recycled to Profit or Loss.

No FCTR is reclassified to Profit or Loss; instead, the proportionate share of cumulative exchange differences (20% of ₹10 Cr = ₹2 Crores) is reattributed to the Non-Controlling Interest (NCI) within equity.
The entire ₹10 Crores FCTR is recycled to P&L.
FCTR is transferred to Capital Reserve.
ref: Ind AS 21 - Paragraph 48A: Partial Disposal of a Subsidiary Without Loss of Control
explanation: Ind AS 21 Paragraph 48A specifies: 'On the partial disposal of a subsidiary that includes a foreign operation, the entity shall re-attribute the proportionate share of the cumulative amount of the exchange differences recognized in other comprehensive income to the non-controlling interests in that foreign operation.' It is an equity transaction; no recycling to P&L occurs.

subject: Financial Reporting
tag: [ICAI CA Final FR PYQ] Ind AS 21: Cumulative Translation Differences in Inter-Company Eliminations
question: Parent Ltd. sells goods to foreign subsidiary Sub Ltd. Sub Ltd. owes Parent Ltd. $5,000,000. In Parent's books (INR functional), an exchange gain of ₹2 Crores arises on this monetary balance. When preparing consolidated financial statements, how is this exchange gain treated?
options: The exchange gain is eliminated in full against consolidated profit.

Because the monetary item represents a commitment to convert one currency into another, it exposes the group to a currency fluctuation risk; therefore, in consolidated financial statements, the exchange difference is NOT eliminated, but continues to be recognized in consolidated Profit or Loss (unless it forms part of a net investment under Paragraph 15).
Recognized in OCI.
Transferred to NCI.
ref: Ind AS 21 - Paragraph 45: Intra-Group Foreign Exchange Differences in Consolidation
explanation: Ind AS 21 Paragraph 45 explains that an intra-group monetary asset or liability cannot be eliminated without showing the results of currency fluctuations in the consolidated financial statements. This is because the monetary item represents a commitment to convert one currency into another and exposes the group to a currency risk. Accordingly, such an exchange difference continues to be recognized in profit or loss.

subject: Financial Reporting
tag: [ICAI CA Final FR PYQ] Ind AS 29: Economy Ceasing to be Hyperinflationary
question: When an economy ceases to be hyperinflationary and an entity discontinues the preparation of financial statements in accordance with Ind AS 29, what is the accounting treatment for carrying amounts?
options: All assets must be restated back to original historical costs before hyperinflation.
The entity shall treat the amounts expressed in the measuring unit current at the end of the previous reporting period as the basis for the carrying amounts in its subsequent financial statements.
All reserves must be capitalized into equity shares.
The entity must liquidate its operating divisions.
ref: Ind AS 29 - Paragraph 38: Cessation of Hyperinflation
explanation: Ind AS 29 Paragraph 38 states: 'When an economy ceases to be hyperinflationary and an entity discontinues the preparation and presentation of financial statements in accordance with this Standard, it shall treat the amounts expressed in the measuring unit current at the end of the previous reporting period as the basis for the carrying amounts in its subsequent financial statements.'

subject: Financial Reporting
tag: [ICAI CA Final FR PYQ] Ind AS 20: Capital Grant Presentation Options
question: GreenEnergy Ltd. receives a Government Grant of ₹20 Crores towards the purchase of a pollution control plant costing ₹100 Crores (useful life 10 years, residual value nil). Under Ind AS 20, what are the two permissible methods of presenting this grant on the balance sheet?
options: Option 1: Credit directly to Equity Share Capital; Option 2: Recognize as immediate revenue in P&L.

Option 1: Present the grant as Deferred Income (which is recognized in profit or loss on a systematic basis over the 10-year useful life of the plant); Option 2: Deduct the grant in arriving at the carrying amount of the asset (reducing initial plant cost to ₹80 Crores, depreciated at ₹8 Crores/year).
Option 1: Credit to Revaluation Reserve; Option 2: Treat as an off-balance sheet item.
Government grants for capital assets cannot be recognized under Ind AS.
ref: Ind AS 20 (Accounting for Government Grants and Disclosure of Government Assistance) - Paragraph 24: Grants Related to Assets
explanation: Ind AS 20 Paragraph 24 provides two methods of presenting grants related to assets in the balance sheet: (a) setting up the grant as deferred income, which is recognized in profit or loss on a systematic basis over the useful life of the asset; or (b) deducting the grant in calculating the carrying amount of the asset (depreciation is charged on the reduced carrying amount).

subject: Financial Reporting
tag: [ICAI CA Final FR PYQ] Ind AS 20: Below-Market Interest Rate Government Loans
question: On 1st April 2023, BioPharma Ltd. receives an interest-free loan of ₹10 Crores from the Department of Biotechnology repayable in full after 5 years. The market borrowing rate for an equivalent commercial loan is 10% per annum (PV factor for 5 years at 10% = 0.6209). How should this loan and government assistance be recorded on 1st April 2023 under Ind AS 109 and Ind AS 20?
options: Record loan liability at full ₹10 Crores with zero government grant recognition.

Measure the financial liability at fair value of ₹6.209 Crores under Ind AS 109; the difference of ₹3.791 Crores between initial cash proceeds and fair value is recognized as a Government Grant (Deferred Income) under Ind AS 20 to be recognized in profit or loss over the period of the loan.
Recognize ₹3.791 Crores immediately as an exceptional gain in P&L.
Record the loan in Other Comprehensive Income.
ref: Ind AS 20 - Paragraph 10A & Ind AS 109: Below-Market Government Loans
explanation: Ind AS 20 Paragraph 10A states: 'The benefit of a government loan at a below-market rate of interest is treated as a government grant. The loan shall be recognized and measured in accordance with Ind AS 109. The benefit of the below-market rate of interest shall be measured as the difference between the initial carrying value of the loan determined in accordance with Ind AS 109 and the proceeds received.' The ₹3.791 Cr benefit is accounted for under Ind AS 20.

subject: Financial Reporting
tag: [ICAI CA Final FR PYQ] Ind AS 20: Repayment of Government Grants
question: Four years ago, Apex Textiles received a government grant of ₹5 Crores towards a factory facility, which was accounted for by deducting the grant from the asset carrying amount. In FY 2023-24, due to a breach of employment covenants, the Government demanded full repayment of the ₹5 Crores grant. How should this repayment be accounted for under Ind AS 20?
options: Recognize full ₹5 Crores as an extraordinary prior period error.

Repayment of a grant related to an asset shall be recognized by increasing the carrying amount of the asset; the cumulative additional depreciation that would have been recognized in profit or loss to date in the absence of the grant shall be recognized immediately in profit or loss.
Deducted directly from retained earnings.
Treated as an expense in OCI.
ref: Ind AS 20 - Paragraph 32: Repayment of Grants Related to an Asset
explanation: Ind AS 20 Paragraph 32 states: 'Repayment of a grant related to an asset shall be recognized by increasing the carrying amount of the asset or reducing the deferred income balance by the amount repayable. The cumulative additional depreciation that would have been recognized in profit or loss to date in the absence of the grant shall be recognized immediately in profit or loss.'

subject: Financial Reporting
tag: [ICAI CA Final FR PYQ] Ind AS 20: Grant Given as Immediate Financial Support for Past Losses
question: During an economic crisis, the State Government issues an unconditional cash grant of ₹10 Crores to AgroMills Ltd. to provide immediate financial relief for severe drought losses incurred in the preceding agricultural season. Under Ind AS 20, how should this grant be recognized?
options: Deferred and recognized over the next 5 years.
Recognized in the Statement of Profit and Loss of the period in which it becomes receivable as an item of income, because it was given as immediate financial support with no future related costs.
Credited directly to Capital Reserve in Equity.
Recognized in OCI.
ref: Ind AS 20 - Paragraph 20: Grant as Immediate Financial Relief
explanation: Ind AS 20 Paragraph 20 states: 'A government grant that becomes receivable as compensation for expenses or losses already incurred or for the purpose of giving immediate financial support to the entity with no future related costs shall be recognized in profit or loss of the period in which it becomes receivable.'

subject: Financial Reporting
tag: [ICAI CA Final FR PYQ] Ind AS 23: Definition of a Qualifying Asset
question: Which of the following assets qualifies as a 'Qualifying Asset' eligible for capitalization of borrowing costs under Ind AS 23?
options: Inventories that are routinely manufactured or produced in large quantities on a repetitive basis over a few hours.

An asset that necessarily takes a substantial period of time to get ready for its intended use or sale (such as a toll bridge taking 3 years to construct or aging single-malt whiskey requiring 12 years of maturation).
Financial assets measured at fair value under Ind AS 109.
Assets that are ready for their intended use or sale when acquired.
ref: Ind AS 23 (Borrowing Costs) - Paragraph 5: Definition of Qualifying Asset
explanation: Ind AS 23 Paragraph 5 defines a qualifying asset as 'an asset that necessarily takes a substantial period of time to get ready for its intended use or sale.' Examples include manufacturing plants, power generation facilities, intangible assets under development, and investment properties under construction. Financial assets and inventories produced over a short period are explicitly excluded.

subject: Financial Reporting
tag: [ICAI CA Final FR PYQ] Ind AS 23: Commencement of Capitalisation Criteria
question: Which three criteria must ALL be satisfied simultaneously for an entity to commence capitalising borrowing costs as part of the cost of a qualifying asset under Ind AS 23?
options: Loan agreement signed, bank disburses funds, and interest is paid.
(a) It incurs expenditures for the asset; (b) it incurs borrowing costs; and (c) it undertakes activities that are necessary to prepare the asset for its intended use or sale.
Board passes a resolution, architectural drawings are finalized, and building permits are applied for.
Statutory auditor inspects the construction site.
ref: Ind AS 23 - Paragraph 17: Commencement of Capitalisation
explanation: Ind AS 23 Paragraph 17 specifies: 'An entity shall begin capitalising borrowing costs as part of the cost of a qualifying asset on the commencement date. The commencement date for capitalisation is the date when the entity first meets all of the following conditions: (a) it incurs expenditures for the asset; (b) it incurs borrowing costs; and (c) it undertakes activities that are necessary to prepare the asset for its intended use or sale.'

subject: Financial Reporting
tag: [ICAI CA Final FR PYQ] Ind AS 23: Temporary Investment Income on Specific Borrowings
question: InfraCorp Ltd. borrows ₹50 Crores specifically to construct a marine drydock on 1st April 2023 at 10% interest. Construction begins immediately. During the first 6 months, ₹20 Crores of surplus borrowed funds not yet needed for site payments were temporarily invested in money market mutual funds, earning interest income of ₹80 Lakhs. What is the net borrowing cost capitalized for the year ended 31st March 2024?
options: ₹5.0 Crores (gross interest of 10% on ₹50 Crores), with ₹80 Lakhs recognized as finance income in P&L.
₹4.2 Crores (Gross borrowing costs incurred of ₹5.0 Crores minus temporary investment income earned of ₹80 Lakhs on specific borrowings).
Zero, because borrowing costs on specific borrowings cannot be capitalized.
₹5.8 Crores.
ref: Ind AS 23 - Paragraph 12: Specific Borrowings & Temporary Investment Income
explanation: Ind AS 23 Paragraph 12 states: 'To the extent that an entity borrows funds specifically for the purpose of obtaining a qualifying asset, the entity shall determine the amount of borrowing costs eligible for capitalisation as the actual borrowing costs incurred on that borrowing during the period less any investment income on the temporary investment of those borrowings.' Eligible = ₹5.0 Cr - ₹0.8 Cr = ₹4.2 Crores.

subject: Financial Reporting
tag: [ICAI CA Final FR PYQ] Ind AS 23: Capitalisation Rate for General Borrowings
question: Titan Ltd. incurs capital expenditure of ₹40 Crores on a qualifying asset during the year, financed through general corporate borrowings. Its general borrowing pool consists of: (i) ₹60 Crores bank loan at 8% p.a. (interest ₹4.8 Cr); and (ii) ₹40 Crores debentures at 10% p.a. (interest ₹4.0 Cr). What is the weighted average capitalization rate and borrowing cost capitalized for the year under Ind AS 23?
options: Rate = 9.0%; Borrowing cost capitalized = ₹3.6 Crores.
Rate = 8.8% (Total interest ₹8.8 Crores / Total general borrowings ₹100 Crores); Borrowing cost capitalized = 8.8% × ₹40 Crores = ₹3.52 Crores.
Rate = 10%; Borrowing cost capitalized = ₹4.0 Crores.
Rate = 8%; Borrowing cost capitalized = ₹3.2 Crores.
ref: Ind AS 23 - Paragraph 14: Capitalisation Rate on General Borrowings
explanation: Under Ind AS 23 Paragraph 14, the capitalization rate shall be the weighted average of the borrowing costs applicable to all borrowings of the entity that are outstanding during the period, other than borrowings made specifically for the purpose of obtaining a qualifying asset. Capitalization rate = ₹8.8 Cr / ₹100 Cr = 8.8%. Capitalized borrowing cost = ₹40 Cr × 8.8% = ₹3.52 Crores.

subject: Financial Reporting
tag: [ICAI CA Final FR PYQ] Ind AS 23: Suspension of Capitalisation During Extended Interruption
question: Construction of a hydroelectric dam is halted for 6 months due to a violent local labor strike and environmental litigation (abnormal stoppage not necessary for the engineering process). How should the borrowing costs incurred during this 6-month idle period be treated under Ind AS 23?
options: Continue capitalising borrowing costs without interruption.

An entity shall suspend capitalisation of borrowing costs during extended periods in which it suspends active development of a qualifying asset; borrowing costs incurred during the 6 months are expensed in Profit or Loss.
Capitalize 50% and expense 50%.
Recognize in OCI.
ref: Ind AS 23 - Paragraphs 20-21: Suspension of Capitalisation
explanation: Ind AS 23 Paragraph 20 states: 'An entity shall suspend capitalisation of borrowing costs during extended periods in which it suspends active development of a qualifying asset.' Paragraph 21 clarifies that capitalisation is not suspended when a temporary delay is a necessary part of the process of getting an asset ready (e.g. high water levels during rainy season in bridge building), but strikes and disputes require suspension.

subject: Financial Reporting
tag: [ICAI CA Final FR PYQ] Ind AS 23: Cessation of Capitalisation for Parts Completed in Stages
question: A commercial real estate park consists of 5 standalone office towers. Tower 1 is structurally finished, air-conditioned, licensed, and ready for commercial leasing on 31st December 2023, while Towers 2 to 5 are still under construction. Can borrowing costs continue to be capitalized on Tower 1 after 31st December 2023?
options: Yes, capitalization continues until all 5 towers of the entire business park are completed.

No, when an entity completes the construction of a qualifying asset in parts and each part is capable of being used while construction continues on other parts, the entity shall cease capitalising borrowing costs when it completes substantially all the activities necessary to prepare that part for its intended use or sale.
Capitalization ceases only when tenants sign lease deeds.
Borrowing costs on Tower 1 must be reversed retrospectively.
ref: Ind AS 23 - Paragraph 24: Cessation of Capitalisation for Assets Completed in Parts
explanation: Ind AS 23 Paragraph 24 specifies: 'When an entity completes the construction of a qualifying asset in parts and each part is capable of being used while construction continues on other parts, the entity shall cease capitalising borrowing costs when it completes substantially all the activities necessary to prepare that part for its intended use or sale.' Capitalization on Tower 1 ceases on 31st December.

subject: Financial Reporting
tag: [ICAI CA Final FR PYQ] Ind AS 20: Non-Monetary Government Grants
question: The State Government allocates 50 acres of prime industrial land to GreenTech Ltd. free of cost to establish a semiconductor wafer fabrication plant. The nominal stamp registration fee paid was ₹10,000. The fair value of the land is appraised at ₹25 Crores by government approved valuers. Under Ind AS 20, how may GreenTech Ltd. account for this non-monetary government grant?
options: Only at the nominal value of ₹10,000.

Under Ind AS 20 Paragraph 23, the entity may account for both the asset and the grant either at the fair value of the non-monetary asset (₹25 Crores land with a corresponding ₹25 Crores deferred government grant) or at a nominal amount (₹10,000).
At ₹25 Crores with a credit to Share Capital.
Non-monetary grants cannot be recognized on the balance sheet.
ref: Ind AS 20 - Paragraph 23: Non-Monetary Government Grants
explanation: Ind AS 20 Paragraph 23 states: 'A government grant may take the form of a transfer of a non-monetary asset, such as land or other resources, for the use of the entity. In these circumstances it is usual to assess the fair value of the non-monetary asset and to account for both grant and asset at that fair value. An alternative course that is sometimes followed is to record both asset and grant at a nominal amount.'

subject: Financial Reporting
tag: [ICAI CA Final FR PYQ] Ind AS 20: Matching Principle for Grants Related to Income
question: SkillIndia Ltd. receives a Government Grant of ₹30 Lakhs in March 2024 to reimburse training costs for underprivileged apprentices. The training program will run across FY 2024-25 and FY 2025-26 (training costs projected at ₹20 Lakhs in Year 1 and ₹40 Lakhs in Year 2). How should the grant be recognized in profit or loss under Ind AS 20?
options: Recognize entire ₹30 Lakhs as income in March 2024 when cash is received.

Recognized in profit or loss on a systematic basis over the periods in which the entity recognizes as expenses the related costs for which the grant is intended to compensate: ₹10 Lakhs in Year 1 (₹20L/₹60L × ₹30L) and ₹20 Lakhs in Year 2 (₹40L/₹60L × ₹30L).
Split equally at ₹15 Lakhs per year.
Credited directly to general reserve.
ref: Ind AS 20 - Paragraph 12: Recognition of Grants Related to Income
explanation: Ind AS 20 Paragraph 12 states: 'Government grants shall be recognized in profit or loss on a systematic basis over the periods in which the entity recognizes as expenses the related costs for which the grants are intended to compensate.' The grant is recognized pro-rata to the incurred training costs.

subject: Financial Reporting
tag: [ICAI CA Final FR PYQ] Ind AS 23: Land Acquisition as Qualifying Asset
question: Urban Developers Ltd. purchases vacant freehold land for ₹100 Crores using bank borrowings. The land is intended to be held for long-term capital appreciation, with no active site development or construction planned in the foreseeable future. Are the borrowing costs on this land loan eligible for capitalization under Ind AS 23?
options: Yes, land is always a qualifying asset under Ind AS 23.

No, borrowing costs incurred on land acquired without any associated development activities are NOT eligible for capitalisation, because the land was ready for its intended use (holding for capital appreciation) when acquired and does not undergo activities necessary to prepare it for intended use.
Yes, up to 10% of land value.
Capitalized only if land is revalued.
ref: Ind AS 23 - Paragraphs 5 & 19: Land without Development is Not a Qualifying Asset
explanation: Ind AS 23 states that an asset is a qualifying asset only if it takes a substantial period of time to get ready for its intended use. Land acquired without development is ready for its intended use when acquired. However, land that is acquired for development (e.g. where substantial earthworks, roads, and utilities are being developed) qualifies while the development activities are ongoing.

subject: Financial Reporting
tag: [ICAI CA Final FR PYQ] Ind AS 20: Forgivable Loans
question: Under a rural industrialization scheme, the Government grants a loan of ₹2 Crores to SmallCrafts Ltd. The terms state that the loan will be forgiven in full if the company maintains continuous operations and employs at least 50 rural artisans for 3 consecutive years. Under Ind AS 20, how is a forgivable loan treated?
options: Treated as permanent equity from day 1.
A forgivable loan from government is treated as a government grant when there is reasonable assurance that the entity will meet the terms for forgiveness of the loan.
Accounted for as a contingent liability.
Ignored until the 3 years elapse.
ref: Ind AS 20 - Paragraph 10: Forgivable Loans as Government Grants
explanation: Ind AS 20 Paragraph 10 states: 'A forgivable loan from government is treated as a government grant when there is reasonable assurance that the entity will meet the terms for forgiveness of the loan.' When reasonable assurance exists, it is accounted for as a grant.

subject: Financial Reporting
tag: [ICAI CA Final FR PYQ] Ind AS 23: Excess Carrying Amount of Qualifying Asset Over Recoverable Amount
question: When the carrying amount or the expected ultimate cost of a qualifying asset (including capitalized borrowing costs) exceeds its recoverable amount or net realizable value, what is the mandatory requirement under Ind AS 23?
options: Capitalization of borrowing costs must be increased to match fair value.
The carrying amount is written down or written off in accordance with the requirements of other Standards (such as Ind AS 36 Impairment of Assets or Ind AS 2 Inventories).
Borrowing costs are moved to Other Comprehensive Income.
Capitalization continues unaffected.
ref: Ind AS 23 - Paragraph 16: Impairment of Qualifying Assets
explanation: Ind AS 23 Paragraph 16 states: 'When the carrying amount or the expected ultimate cost of the qualifying asset exceeds its recoverable amount or net realizable value, the carrying amount is written down or written off in accordance with the requirements of other Standards. In certain circumstances, the amount of the write-down or write-off is written back in accordance with those other Standards.'

subject: Financial Reporting
tag: [ICAI CA Final FR PYQ] Ind AS 20: Government Assistance without Quantifiable Value
question: The Ministry of Heavy Industries provides free technical advisory assistance and sanitary quarantine consultation to automotive exporters, but the service cannot reasonably have a value placed upon it. Under Ind AS 20, how should this government assistance be treated?
options: Valued at management's best estimate and recorded as revenue.
Excluded from financial values on the balance sheet and P&L, but disclosed in the notes to financial statements, specifying the nature, extent, and duration of the government assistance.
Omitted completely with zero disclosure.
Recorded in equity.
ref: Ind AS 20 - Paragraphs 34-36: Government Assistance Disclosures
explanation: Ind AS 20 Paragraph 34 notes that government assistance may take forms which cannot reasonably have a value placed upon them (e.g. free technical or marketing advice). Such assistance is disclosed in the notes so that the financial statements are not misleading.

subject: Financial Reporting
tag: [ICAI CA Final FR PYQ] Ind AS 23: Group Borrowings and Subsidiary Capitalisation Rate
question: Parent Ltd. raises general borrowings at 8% and passes the funds to its subsidiary Sub Ltd. at 10% to construct a qualifying asset. In Sub Ltd.'s separate financial statements and in the group's consolidated financial statements, what interest rate is used to capitalize borrowing costs?
options: 10% in both separate and consolidated financial statements.

In Sub Ltd.'s separate financial statements, 10% (the actual borrowing cost incurred by the subsidiary); in the group's consolidated financial statements, 8% (the actual external borrowing cost incurred by the economic entity).
8% in both separate and consolidated statements.
Borrowing costs between group entities cannot be capitalized.
ref: Ind AS 23 - Group Financial Statements & Borrowing Costs
explanation: In separate financial statements, the borrowing cost to the subsidiary is its contractual cost (10%). In consolidated financial statements, intercompany interest is eliminated, and the borrowing cost capitalized cannot exceed the actual borrowing cost incurred by the group from external lenders (8%).

subject: Financial Reporting
tag: [ICAI CA Final FR PYQ] Ind AS 20: Export Incentive Scrips (RoDTEP / MEIS)
question: An exporter earns Remission of Duties and Taxes on Exported Products (RoDTEP) scrips from the Directorate General of Foreign Trade (DGFT) upon exporting goods. When should the government grant scrips be recognized under Ind AS 20?
options: Only when the scrips are physically utilized to clear import customs duty.
When there is reasonable assurance that the entity will comply with the conditions attached to them (export of eligible goods) and the grants will be received (assessed at the date of export).
When the scrips are sold to a third party for cash.
At the end of the financial year.
ref: Ind AS 20 - Paragraph 7: Recognition on Reasonable Assurance
explanation: Under Ind AS 20 Paragraph 7, government grants, including non-monetary grants, shall not be recognized until there is reasonable assurance that: (a) the entity will comply with the conditions attaching to them; and (b) the grants will be received. For export incentives, recognition occurs upon completion of export performance.

subject: Financial Reporting
tag: [ICAI CA Final FR PYQ] Ind AS 23: Exchange Rate Gains Exceeding Actual Borrowing Costs
question: An entity borrows USD at 4% interest to construct a plant. During the year, INR appreciates sharply against USD, resulting in a foreign exchange gain of ₹2 Crores. Total interest paid was ₹1.5 Crores. Can the net negative borrowing cost of ₹0.5 Crores be credited to the cost of the asset under Ind AS 23?
options: Yes, reducing asset cost below actual construction expenditures.

No, borrowing costs eligible for capitalisation cannot be negative; exchange gains can offset foreign currency interest expense up to the amount of interest incurred, and any excess exchange gain is recognized in profit or loss under Ind AS 21.
Yes, credited to revaluation reserve.
Deferred to the next financial year.
ref: Ind AS 23 & Ind AS 21: Exchange Differences as Borrowing Costs Limitation
explanation: Exchange differences are treated as borrowing costs only to the extent they are an adjustment to interest costs. An exchange gain can reduce the foreign currency borrowing cost to zero, but cannot turn the borrowing cost negative to reduce the physical cost of the asset below zero interest.

subject: Financial Reporting
tag: [ICAI CA Final FR PYQ] Ind AS 20: Presentation of Revenue Grants
question: Sun Pharma receives a ₹5 Crores government grant as an operational wage subsidy for hiring local apprentices. Under Ind AS 20, how can this grant related to income be presented in the Statement of Profit and Loss?
options: Only as a credit to Retained Earnings.
Either presented separately under 'Other Operating Income' (or 'Other Income'), or deducted in reporting the related employee benefit expense.
Must be deducted from sales turnover.
Presented in Other Comprehensive Income.
ref: Ind AS 20 - Paragraphs 29-31: Presentation of Grants Related to Income
explanation: Ind AS 20 Paragraph 29 states that grants related to income are presented as part of profit or loss, either separately or under a general heading such as 'Other Income'; alternatively, they are deducted in reporting the related expense. Both methods are regarded as acceptable.

subject: Financial Reporting
tag: [ICAI CA Final FR PYQ] Ind AS 108: Management Approach & Chief Operating Decision Maker (CODM)
question: Under Ind AS 108, how is an 'Operating Segment' identified, and who constitutes the Chief Operating Decision Maker (CODM)?
options: Identified based on statutory tax reporting circles; CODM is always the statutory auditor.

Identified using the 'Management Approach' based on internal organizational units whose operating results are regularly reviewed by the CODM (a function, not necessarily a title, which allocates resources and assesses performance of segments).
Identified strictly by physical geographic pin codes.
Identified based on products with identical gross profit margins.
ref: Ind AS 108 (Operating Segments) - Paragraphs 5-7: Definition of Operating Segment & CODM
explanation: Ind AS 108 Paragraph 5 defines an operating segment as a component of an entity: (a) that engages in business activities from which it may earn revenues and incur expenses; (b) whose operating results are regularly reviewed by the entity's Chief Operating Decision Maker (CODM) to make decisions about resources and assess performance; and (c) for which discrete financial information is available. The CODM is a function that allocates resources.

subject: Financial Reporting
tag: [ICAI CA Final FR PYQ] Ind AS 108: Quantitative Thresholds (10% Tests)
question: A conglomerate has 6 internal operating divisions. Under Ind AS 108 Paragraph 13, which of the following quantitative thresholds mandates that an operating segment must be reported separately?
options: Its reported revenue (including both internal and external sales) is 10% or more of the combined revenue of all operating segments.

The absolute amount of its reported profit or loss is 10% or more of the greater, in absolute amount, of: (i) the combined reported profit of all operating segments that did not report a loss; and (ii) the combined reported loss of all operating segments that reported a loss.
Its assets are 10% or more of the combined assets of all operating segments.
Meeting ANY ONE of the three 10% criteria (Revenue, Profit/Loss, or Assets) makes the segment reportable.
ref: Ind AS 108 - Paragraph 13: The 10% Quantitative Thresholds
explanation: Ind AS 108 Paragraph 13 specifies that an entity shall report separately information about an operating segment that meets any of the following quantitative thresholds: (a) revenue (internal + external) >= 10% of combined revenue; (b) profit/loss >= 10% of the greater of combined profitable segments and combined loss segments; or (c) assets >= 10% of combined assets.

subject: Financial Reporting
tag: [ICAI CA Final FR PYQ] Ind AS 108: The 75% External Revenue Sufficiency Rule
question: After applying the 10% quantitative thresholds, a conglomerate's reportable segments account for only 60% of total consolidated external revenue. What action is required under Ind AS 108 Paragraph 15?
options: No action; remaining 40% is omitted.

Additional operating segments must be identified as reportable segments (even if they do not meet the 10% thresholds) until at least 75% of the entity's total external revenue is included in reportable segments.
The entity must prepare financial statements on a single-segment basis.
The threshold is relaxed to 50% for Indian entities.
ref: Ind AS 108 - Paragraph 15: The 75% External Revenue Threshold
explanation: Ind AS 108 Paragraph 15 explicitly mandates: 'If the total external revenue reported by operating segments constitutes less than 75% of the entity's revenue, additional operating segments shall be identified as reportable segments (even if they do not meet the criteria in paragraph 13) until at least 75% of the entity's revenue is included in reportable segments.'

subject: Financial Reporting
tag: [ICAI CA Final FR PYQ] Ind AS 108: Major Customer Disclosure Threshold
question: Under Ind AS 108, when is an entity required to disclose information about its reliance on major customers?
options: When any single customer accounts for more than 1% of total revenues.

If revenues from transactions with a single external customer amount to 10% or more of an entity's total revenues, the entity shall disclose that fact, the total amount of revenues from each such customer, and the identity of the segment(s) reporting the revenues (the name of the customer need not be disclosed).
Only when the customer is a government ministry.
Major customer disclosures are prohibited for confidentiality.
ref: Ind AS 108 - Paragraph 34: Information About Major Customers
explanation: Ind AS 108 Paragraph 34 states: 'If revenues from transactions with a single external customer amount to 10 per cent or more of an entity's revenues, the entity shall disclose that fact, the total amount of revenues from each such customer, and the identity of the segment or segments reporting the revenues. The entity need not disclose the identity of a major customer or the amount of revenues that each segment reports from that customer.'

subject: Financial Reporting
tag: [ICAI CA Final FR PYQ] Ind AS 34: Effective Annual Tax Rate in Interim Reporting
question: Under Ind AS 34, how should interim income tax expense be measured and recognized?
options: Calculated by applying statutory tax slabs to the actual profit of each individual interim quarter without regard to annual forecasts.
Measured using the best estimate of the weighted average annual effective income tax rate expected for the full financial year applied to the pre-tax income of the interim period.
Income tax is recognized only in the fourth quarter when the final tax return is filed.
Measured as a flat 25% of interim EBITDA.
ref: Ind AS 34 (Interim Financial Reporting) - Paragraphs 30(c) & Appendix B Paragraph B12
explanation: Ind AS 34 states that interim period income tax expense is accrued using the tax rate that would be applicable to expected total annual earnings, that is, the estimated average annual effective income tax rate applied to the pre-tax income of the interim period. This reflects the principle that taxes are assessed on an annual basis.

subject: Financial Reporting
tag: [ICAI CA Final FR PYQ] Ind AS 34: Uneven and Seasonal Revenues in Interim Periods
question: A ski resort and winter clothing manufacturer earns 85% of its annual sales revenues in Quarter 3 (October to December). How should revenue be recognized in interim financial statements under Ind AS 34?
options: Anticipated annual revenues must be averaged and smoothed equally across all 4 quarters.

Revenues that are received seasonally, cyclically, or occasionally within a financial year shall NOT be anticipated or deferred for interim reporting purposes unless anticipation or deferral would also be appropriate at the end of the financial year (revenues are recognized when earned in Quarter 3).
Quarter 1 and 2 revenues must be boosted by a management estimate.
Interim reporting is prohibited for seasonal businesses.
ref: Ind AS 34 - Paragraph 37: Revenues Received Seasonally, Cyclically, or Occasionally
